summary: Audit SecureInbox UI surface-by-surface through an Apple-grade premium design lens, then synthesize a sequenced upgrade plan

findings.currentStateSummary: The foundation lives almost entirely in `frontend/src/index.css` via Tailwind v4's `@theme` block (no tailwind.config.* file exists — confirmed). It's a competent, well-organized starting point: a coherent deep-navy dark palette, semantic risk tokens that components correctly reference (never hardcoded), a 4-step radius ramp, and Inter loaded from Google Fonts. However, it stops at "sensible defaults": there is NO custom typographic scale (the app leans on Tailwind's stock sizes, and usage is dominated by `text-sm`/`text-xs` — 45 and 34 hits — so almost everything is small and flat with no real ramp), NO elevation/shadow token system (components sprinkle stock `shadow-sm`/`shadow-lg`/`shadow-2xl` which on a near-black bg are nearly invisible and inconsistent), NO motion tokens (easing/duration are ad-hoc; only one `duration-200` in the whole app), and NO spacing scale beyond Tailwind defaults. Inter is also loaded as a render-blocking stylesheet without `font-display: swap` guaranteed via the link, no variable font, no `font-feature-settings`. The risk palette is functional but its "soft" backgrounds are extremely dark and the danger reds (`#f43f5e` quarantine, `#b91c1c` phishing, `#ef5350` destructive) are three competing reds with no deliberate harmony. This is a clean B-grade foundation; it is not yet Apple-grade because it lacks the deliberate type ramp, elevation language, motion vocabulary, and font polish that make a system feel designed rather than defaulted.

findings.title: No typographic scale defined — app runs on Tailwind defaults and lives almost entirely at text-sm/text-xs
findings.current: @theme only sets --font-sans. There is no --text-* ramp, no line-height or letter-spacing tokens. Usage survey: text-sm (45), text-xs (34), text-xl (5), text-2xl (3), text-base (2), text-lg (1). The largest type in the app is text-2xl (24px).
findings.problem: There is no intentional type ramp — the UI is overwhelmingly 12-14px with one occasional 24px jump, which reads as dense and utilitarian, the opposite of Apple's clarity-through-hierarchy. Apple HIG uses a deliberate, large-stepped ramp (e.g. Large Title 34, Title 28/22, Body 17) where size + weight + tracking together encode hierarchy. Here hierarchy is carried almost entirely by font-weight (font-medium 24, font-semibold 17) because the sizes barely differ.
findings.recommendation: Define a real semantic ramp in @theme and use it everywhere. Suggested (rem at 16px root): --text-display: 2.5rem (40/1.05/-0.02em), --text-h1: 1.875rem (30/1.1/-0.018em), --text-h2: 1.375rem (22/1.2/-0.012em), --text-h3: 1.0625rem (17/1.3/-0.006em), --text-body: 0.9375rem (15/1.5/0), --text-sm: 0.8125rem (13/1.45/0), --text-caption: 0.75rem (12/1.4/+0.01em). Bump default body from 14px to 15px. Pair each step with line-height + letter-spacing so tightening is automatic, then drive headings off these tokens instead of raw text-2xl/text-xl.

findings.title: No elevation/shadow token system — stock shadow-sm/lg/2xl are inconsistent and nearly invisible on #0a0d14
findings.current: No --shadow-* tokens. Components use raw Tailwind shadows ad-hoc: card.jsx shadow-sm, dropdown-menu.jsx shadow-lg, switch.jsx shadow-lg, AppShell.jsx shadow-md, LoginPage.jsx shadow-2xl, input.jsx shadow-sm. Tailwind's default shadows are black with low alpha and disappear against a near-black background.
findings.problem: Apple's depth principle relies on subtle, consistent layering. Here elevation is random per-component and effectively invisible, so cards float on the same plane as the background and the popover/dropdown don't read as lifted. There's also no use of the --color-elevated (#161d2b) token that was defined but is essentially unused for actual elevation.
findings.recommendation: Add a dark-tuned elevation ramp in @theme: --shadow-xs: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4); --shadow-sm: 0 2px 8px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); --shadow-md: 0 8px 24px -6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55); --shadow-lg: 0 16px 48px -12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6). On dark UIs also encode elevation as a subtle top inner highlight + surface lightening: e.g. cards get inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.04) plus a lift to --color-elevated. Map card→shadow-sm, dropdown/popover→shadow-md, modal/login→shadow-lg consistently.

findings.title: No motion tokens — easing and duration are ad-hoc (single duration-200 in entire app)
findings.current: No --ease-* or --duration-* variables. Across src/, transition usage is transition-colors (17), transition (5), transition-transform (2), transition-all (2), transition-opacity (1), and exactly one duration-200. Framer Motion is installed but no shared spring/easing config exists in the foundation.
findings.problem: Premium 'effortless' feel comes from a consistent motion vocabulary — same spring physics and timing everywhere. Right now motion is whatever each component happens to inherit (mostly the browser default ~150ms ease for transition-colors). There's no standard for hover, press, enter/exit, or layout transitions, so nothing feels deliberately tuned.
findings.recommendation: Define motion tokens in @theme: --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) (Apple-like decel), --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1), --duration-fast: 120ms, --duration-base: 200ms, --duration-slow: 320ms. Export a shared Framer spring (e.g. { type: 'spring', stiffness: 420, damping: 34, mass: 0.9 }) from a lib/motion.js so all components share one physics. Standardize: hover 120ms, press scale 0.97 with spring, list/route enter with the spring + 8px y-offset.

findings.title: Inter loaded render-blocking from Google Fonts, static weights, no variable font, no font-feature-settings
findings.current: <link href="...Inter:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap"> as a blocking stylesheet (preconnect present, but the CSS link is not preloaded). Only 4 static weights. index.css:78-81 sets antialiased + optimizeLegibility but no font-feature-settings; tabular-nums is applied per-component (8 spots) rather than globally configured.
findings.problem: A premium product self-hosts a variable font for instant, jank-free rendering and full weight range (incl. 450/500 optical nuance), and enables Inter's stylistic refinements. Relying on Google Fonts adds a network round-trip and a FOUT, and the missing cv/ss feature settings leave Inter looking like the generic default rather than the polished version (e.g. the default single-story 'a'/'g', non-disambiguated 'I'/'l').
findings.recommendation: Self-host Inter variable (InterVariable.woff2) and preload it: <link rel="preload" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>. Define @font-face with font-display: swap and font-weight: 100 900. In index.css body add font-feature-settings: 'cv11','ss01','cv01'; and font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums for UI numerals (or scope tabular to data). Consider Inter Display for >24px headings. This removes the third-party dependency and the FOUT entirely.

findings.title: Risk 'soft' background tokens are too dark to read as tinted surfaces
findings.current: --color-risk-safe-soft #14271d, review-soft #2a2310, quarantine-soft #2a1020, phishing-soft #220d0d, unscanned-soft #1a2130. These are used in risk.js TONES as the badge/banner fill (e.g. soft: 'bg-risk-quarantine-soft text-risk-quarantine border ...').
findings.problem: On the #0a0d14 background these soft fills are only marginally lighter than the page, so risk badges/banners read as near-black chips with colored text rather than confident tinted pills. The intended at-a-glance color coding (the whole point of a 6-bucket security overlay) is muted. Quarantine-soft #2a1020 in particular is barely distinguishable from phishing-soft #220d0d.
findings.recommendation: Either lift the soft tones to ~12-15% luminance with more chroma (e.g. quarantine-soft #3a1622, review-soft #3a3015, safe-soft #18331f) or — cleaner for a token system — derive them at usage time with color-mix so they're always in lockstep with the base hue, e.g. background: color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-risk-quarantine) 14%, var(--color-background)). Test each against AA for the colored text that sits on it.

findings.title: Three competing reds with no deliberate harmony (quarantine vs phishing vs destructive)
findings.current: --color-destructive #ef5350 (warm coral red), --color-risk-quarantine #f43f5e (rose/pink red), --color-risk-phishing #b91c1c (dark brick red). All three appear in the UI simultaneously (destructive buttons, quarantine badges, confirmed-phishing badges).
findings.problem: These three reds come from different hue families (coral ~5°, rose ~350°, brick ~0° but very dark) and don't form a designed scale, so the danger language looks accidental rather than systematic. For a security tool, the escalation quarantine → confirmed phishing should feel like one deliberate ramp, and destructive actions shouldn't clash with risk colors. This also risks 'drowning the UI in alarm-red' (the explicit anti-goal) because the reds are loud and unrelated.
findings.recommendation: Pick one red hue family and build a deliberate severity ramp in OKLCH: e.g. quarantine = oklch(0.62 0.20 18) ~#f0506b, confirmed_phishing = oklch(0.50 0.20 22) ~#c43030 (same hue, darker/denser = more severe). Set --color-destructive to a desaturated version of the same family (oklch(0.58 0.16 20)) so action-red is visibly calmer than risk-red. Reserve the most saturated, darkest red strictly for confirmed phishing.

findings.title: Radius ramp lacks a tactile small step and the values don't match shadcn component usage
findings.current: --radius-sm 0.375rem(6px), --radius-md 0.5rem(8px), --radius-lg 0.75rem(12px), --radius-xl 1rem(16px). Components use a wider range than the ramp exposes: rounded-full (16), rounded-lg (14), rounded-md (11), rounded (6), rounded-xl (5), rounded-2xl (3) — so rounded-2xl (LoginPage) and bare rounded (4px) fall outside the defined tokens.
findings.problem: The ramp is reasonable but (a) it's missing the very small and very large steps the app actually uses (rounded-2xl/16px+, and a crisp 4px), so designers reach for off-system Tailwind defaults, and (b) there's no single source --radius that the others derive from, which is the idiomatic shadcn pattern. The result is six different radii in play without a governing relationship.
findings.recommendation: Define a base and derive: --radius: 0.625rem (10px); then --radius-sm: calc(var(--radius) - 4px), --radius-md: calc(var(--radius) - 2px), --radius-lg: var(--radius), --radius-xl: calc(var(--radius) + 6px), --radius-2xl: calc(var(--radius) + 14px). Pick concentric defaults: inputs/buttons --radius-md(~8px), cards --radius-lg(~10px), modals/login --radius-2xl(~24px), pills rounded-full. Remove bare `rounded` usages in favor of a named step.

findings.title: No spacing scale or vertical rhythm tokens — only container-page exists
findings.current: The only spacing primitive is the container-page utility (max-width 80rem, padding-inline 1.5rem). No section-spacing, stack, or content-gutter tokens; all spacing is per-component Tailwind values.
findings.problem: Apple-grade layouts feel calm because of consistent, generous rhythm (section gaps, content gutters, stack spacing) applied from a shared scale. Without spacing tokens, padding/gaps drift component to component and the foundation can't enforce the generous whitespace the design goal calls for.
findings.recommendation: Add semantic spacing tokens in @theme: --space-section: 2.5rem, --space-block: 1.5rem, --space-stack: 0.75rem, --gutter: 1.5rem (and bump container-page padding to clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2rem) for breathing room on large screens). Optionally widen container-page to allow a comfortable reading column for email bodies. Expose a `stack`/`section` utility so vertical rhythm is one source of truth.

findings.title: tracking-wider used for labels but no defined uppercase-label token / eyebrow style
findings.current: tracking-wider (3), tracking-wide (1), tracking-tight (3) used ad-hoc. There's no defined 'overline/eyebrow' style (uppercase + tracking + size + muted color) even though the pattern appears.
findings.problem: Small uppercase section labels are a signature of clean, premium UIs, but here each instance hand-rolls tracking + size + case + color, so they're inconsistent. The foundation doesn't codify this very common micro-pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add an @utility label-overline { font-size: 0.6875rem; line-height: 1; letter-spacing: 0.08em; text-transform: uppercase; font-weight: 600; color: var(--color-muted-foreground); } and use it for all section eyebrows. Pairs naturally with the new type ramp.

findings.title: muted-foreground #8a96aa likely fails AA on card surfaces at small sizes
findings.current: --color-muted-foreground #8a96aa on --color-card #11151f and --color-background #0a0d14. This color is the default for the abundant text-xs/text-sm secondary text (34+45 usages).
findings.problem: #8a96aa on #11151f is roughly a 4.6:1 contrast — passes AA for normal text but is borderline, and on the darker #0a0d14 with 12px text it gets risky for the large volume of small secondary text. Premium + accessible means comfortable margins, not just barely passing.
findings.recommendation: Lighten muted-foreground to ~#9aa6ba (≈5.5:1 on card) for body-secondary, and introduce a distinct --color-muted-foreground-subtle (~#6b7689) reserved for truly tertiary/disabled text so the two roles aren't collapsed into one borderline value. Verify with a contrast checker against both card and background.

findings.title: Border-color applied to the universal selector — fragile and overrides intent
findings.current: @layer base { * { border-color: var(--color-border); } }
findings.problem: Setting border-color on every element (the shadcn v3 idiom) is heavy-handed in Tailwind v4 where you can default the border color via the theme, and it can quietly override risk border-l-* intentions or any component that expects the browser default. It's a foundation-level smell that can cause subtle, hard-to-debug border color bugs.
findings.recommendation: Prefer Tailwind v4's approach: rely on the border utilities reading --color-border, and scope the reset more tightly (e.g. *, ::before, ::after only where you actually add borders) or drop it. At minimum confirm risk border-l-risk-* utilities still win specificity.

findings.title: Primary #3b9eff is a flat single value — no tonal scale and no hover/active tokens
findings.current: --color-primary #3b9eff with only --color-primary-foreground. Hover is done via opacity (button.jsx: hover:bg-primary/90). No primary-50..900 scale, no separate hover/active token, no subtle primary-tinted surface token beyond ad-hoc bg-primary/10, /15.
findings.problem: Opacity-based hover (primary/90) muddies the color against the dark bg rather than producing a crisp brighter/darker press state, and there's no canonical primary surface tint (the /5,/10,/15 variants are scattered). A premium brand color usually ships as a small tonal scale so hover, active, focus-ring, and tinted backgrounds are all deliberate.
findings.recommendation: Add --color-primary-hover (slightly brighter, e.g. #57adff), --color-primary-active (#2a8be6), and --color-primary-soft (a defined tint, e.g. color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-primary) 12%, var(--color-background))). Switch button hover from /90 opacity to the explicit --color-primary-hover. Consider deepening primary-foreground contrast (current #04111f is good) and tuning the focus --color-ring to a slightly lighter primary for visibility.

premiumOpportunities: Ship a true variable-font-driven type system: self-host InterVariable, expose a semantic ramp (--text-display through --text-caption) with paired line-height/tracking, and let a single optical weight (e.g. 460 for body, 600 for headings) carry the 'designed by Apple' calm. The whole app inherits it for free — biggest single ROI on this surface.

Define a depth/material language as tokens: combine the unused --color-elevated with a dark-tuned shadow ramp AND a top inner-highlight (inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.04)) so every card, popover, and the login modal share one believable lift. Add an optional 'glass' token (background blur + translucent surface + hairline border) for the app shell/top bar to get Apple-style deference where chrome floats over content.

Create a shared motion foundation (lib/motion.js) exporting one spring and the --ease/--duration tokens, then wire a signature 'verdict reveal': when a scan completes, the risk badge springs in with its tinted soft surface and a subtle one-shot pulse of the risk hue — calm, single, intentional, never looping. This makes the core security moment feel tactile and trustworthy.

Build the risk palette in OKLCH as ONE deliberate severity ramp (safe → suspicious → quarantine → confirmed phishing) where increasing severity = same/related hue with rising chroma and falling lightness, so the escalation reads as a single designed gradient rather than five unrelated colors — and derive all soft/border/text variants from the base via color-mix so the system stays in perfect lockstep and is impossible to drift.

Add a light-mode token layer behind a [data-theme] / prefers-color-scheme switch built on the same semantic tokens (the current architecture is dark-only via color-scheme: dark). Even if dark stays default, having the foundation be theme-aware is a hallmark of a mature, premium design system and future-proofs the thesis demo.

findings.area: App shell, sidebar, navigation, page transitions
findings.currentStateSummary: The shell is a clean, conventional two-pane layout: a 208px (w-52) sticky sidebar on desktop with brand block, four nav links, a Gmail account/sync footer, and a user dropdown; a fixed 64px bottom tab bar on mobile; a floating mobile sync FAB; and a 150ms opacity+y page transition. It is competent and content-first, but it reads as a generic shadcn/Tailwind dashboard rather than an Apple-grade product. The active nav state is a flat tinted pill with no depth, motion, or layered indicator; hover/press feedback is purely color-swap with no tactile spring; the page transition is a single short tween shared across all routes with no scroll reset and no reduced-motion guard. Branding is dense and slightly cramped (two stacked text lines plus an 11px subtitle), the chrome lacks the translucency/depth that would let content recede, and PageHeader.jsx exists but is never imported — every page hand-rolls its own header, so global title hierarchy is inconsistent.

findings.title: Active nav item is a flat tinted block with no depth or shared-layout motion
findings.current: NavLink active state is `bg-primary/15 text-primary`; inactive is `text-muted-foreground hover:bg-accent hover:text-accent-foreground`, with only `transition-colors`. The selected pill snaps on instantly and there is no indicator that travels between items.
findings.problem: The signature Apple-grade navigation cue is a single highlight that physically glides between destinations (the macOS sidebar / iOS tab selection). Here selection just hard-cuts the background color of whichever link is active — there is no continuity, no depth, and the 15%-opacity primary fill on a dark card reads as a weak wash rather than an intentional, confident selection. It feels like default shadcn, not a crafted security product.
findings.recommendation: Add a shared-element indicator using Framer Motion `layoutId`. Render the active background as an absolutely-positioned `motion.div` with `layoutId="nav-active"`, `transition={{ type:'spring', stiffness:380, damping:32 }}`, behind the icon+label. Style it as `bg-primary/12` with a 1px inset border `border-primary/25` and a faint `shadow-[0_1px_0_rgba(255,255,255,0.04)_inset]` for depth. Keep label color crossfade at 180ms. Optionally add a 3px left accent bar (`bg-primary` rounded-full, h-4 centered) that also shares the layoutId so the cue travels vertically between items.

findings.title: Hover/press has no tactile feedback — color-only, no scale or spring
findings.current: Sidebar links use only `transition-colors`; bottom-nav items have no whileTap/active scale at all. The mobile sync FAB (AppShell.jsx:20) only transitions opacity. Nothing responds to press.
findings.problem: Apple interfaces always acknowledge touch/press with a subtle compression. On both desktop hover and especially mobile tap, these targets feel inert — there's no sense you 'pressed' anything, which undercuts the trustworthy, tactile quality a security tool should project.
findings.recommendation: Wrap nav targets in `motion` and add `whileTap={{ scale: 0.96 }}` with `transition={{ type:'spring', stiffness:500, damping:30 }}`. On the bottom-nav icon chip add `whileTap={{ scale: 0.9 }}`. For desktop sidebar hover, animate the indicator/background opacity over 150ms ease-out and lift label color from muted to foreground. Give the mobile sync FAB `whileTap={{ scale: 0.92 }}` and an active state.

findings.title: Page transition is a single shared tween — no scroll reset, no reduced-motion guard, no per-route intent
findings.current: All routes animate identically: `opacity 0→1`, `y 6→0`, exit `y -4`, `duration: 0.15, ease:'easeOut'`. Keyed on `location.pathname`. There is no `useReducedMotion`, and grep shows no ScrollRestoration/scrollTo anywhere — navigating preserves prior scroll position.
findings.problem: 150ms easeOut is a flat, slightly cheap fade; Apple transitions use spring physics and feel like content settling, not blinking. More importantly, drilling Inbox→EmailDetail→back uses the same generic up-fade as switching top-level tabs, so hierarchy is invisible. The missing scroll reset means a long Inbox then opening an email can land you mid-page. No reduced-motion support is an accessibility gap.
findings.recommendation: Switch to spring: `transition={{ type:'spring', stiffness:260, damping:30, mass:0.9 }}` with a slightly larger `y: 10→0`. Gate it: `const reduce = useReducedMotion();` and when true use `{opacity:[0,1]}` with `duration:0.001` (no y). Add scroll reset on pathname change (`window.scrollTo({top:0})` or a `<ScrollToTop>` effect in AppShell). For depth, differentiate detail navigation: detail routes slide-in from x:24 / parent slides to x:-24, so drilling-down reads as forward motion.

findings.title: Sidebar chrome doesn't recede — no translucency/blur, opaque flat card
findings.current: `<aside class="... border-r border-border bg-card/40 ...">` — a solid-ish 40% card fill with a hard 1px border and no backdrop blur, despite the mobile BottomNav (BottomNav.jsx:14) correctly using `bg-card/95 backdrop-blur`.
findings.problem: Apple's 'deference' principle wants chrome to feel like frosted material layered over content, not a separate opaque panel. The desktop sidebar is flatter and more opaque than the mobile nav, which is inconsistent. The hard `border-border` divider is also heavier than needed for a calm tool.
findings.recommendation: Make it material: `bg-card/60 backdrop-blur-xl supports-[backdrop-filter]:bg-card/45`, and soften the divider to `border-r border-white/[0.06]` (or `border-border/50`). Add a faint inner highlight at the top edge (`shadow-[inset_-1px_0_0_rgba(255,255,255,0.03)]`). This makes the shell recede and feel like depth-layered glass.

findings.title: PageHeader component exists but is never used — title hierarchy is inconsistent across pages
findings.current: PageHeader exports a `text-xl font-semibold tracking-tight` title + muted description + actions row, but grep shows zero imports. EmailDetailPage uses `text-xl font-semibold leading-snug`; Reports/Inbox/Dashboard each hand-roll their own top regions with differing sizes and spacing.
findings.problem: Without a single header primitive, every page invents its own type size, weight, and spacing, so the global typographic rhythm drifts — the antithesis of Apple's consistent, predictable hierarchy. Dead code also signals an unfinished system.
findings.recommendation: Adopt PageHeader on every page (Dashboard, Inbox, Reports, Settings, EmailDetail) so titles share one scale. Bump the title to a true display size — `text-2xl font-semibold tracking-[-0.02em]` (28px is the Apple large-title cadence at this density) and standardize description to `text-sm text-muted-foreground`. Render it inside the shell's `max-w-6xl` column with consistent `mb-6`. Delete or wire up; do not leave it orphaned.

findings.title: Brand block is cramped and the product name is overloaded
findings.current: A 36px (h-9) primary-tint square icon next to two stacked lines: `text-sm font-semibold` 'XAI Phishing Shield' and an `text-[11px]` 'SecureInbox' subtitle, with `gap-2.5` and `py-5`.
findings.problem: The 14px wordmark wraps awkwardly in a 208px rail and competes with the subtitle; two names (XAI Phishing Shield + SecureInbox) for one product is confusing and visually noisy at the top of the chrome where calm confidence should set the tone. The mark itself is a plain tinted square, not a memorable brand moment.
findings.recommendation: Pick one name as primary. Show a single wordmark line `text-[15px] font-semibold tracking-[-0.01em]` ('SecureInbox') with the icon, and drop the secondary line (or demote it to a tiny tag only in Settings/About). Give the logo chip more presence: `h-9 w-9 rounded-xl bg-gradient-to-br from-primary/25 to-primary/10 text-primary ring-1 ring-primary/20`. Increase brand-to-nav breathing room with `pt-6 pb-4`.

findings.title: Bottom nav active state only colors the icon chip — no shared indicator, no safe-area inset
findings.current: `fixed ... h-16 ... bg-card/95 backdrop-blur`; active item gets `text-primary` and the icon chip gets `bg-primary/15`. No `whileTap`, no animated indicator, and no `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` padding. AppShell main uses `pb-24` and the MobileSync FAB is hardcoded at `bottom-[72px]`.
findings.problem: On iPhones with a home indicator the 64px bar sits flush against the gesture area with no inset, so labels/touch crowd the bottom edge. The active chip pops in with a hard color cut (no motion), and the FAB's `bottom-[72px]` is a magic number coupled to the bar height that will break if the bar changes. Overall it reads as a basic tab bar, not iOS-grade.
findings.recommendation: Add `pb-[env(safe-area-inset-bottom)]` to the nav and increase effective height; replace `pb-24` / `bottom-[72px]` with values that account for the inset (e.g. FAB at `bottom-[calc(72px+env(safe-area-inset-bottom))]`). Add a `motion.span layoutId="tab-active"` pill behind the active icon chip with a spring (`stiffness:400, damping:30`) and `whileTap={{ scale:0.9 }}` on the chip. Animate label color 150ms.

findings.title: Sidebar density and target sizing are slightly tight and unbalanced
findings.current: Nav uses `space-y-1`, items `px-3 py-2.5` (~40px tall) with 18px icons; the Gmail/user footer sections use much smaller `text-xs`/`text-[11px]`/`text-[10px]` type and tighter padding, with three stacked hairline dividers (`border-t` at lines 70, 101).
findings.problem: The vertical rhythm jumps from comfortable 40px nav rows to a dense cluster of 10-12px footer text crammed against three separate hairlines — the bottom third of the rail feels noisy and unconsidered next to the clean nav. Apple rails keep one consistent rhythm and let dividers be near-invisible.
findings.recommendation: Standardize nav rows to `py-2.5` with `gap-3` (good) but add `space-y-0.5` only if using the moving indicator. Lift footer type: Gmail email to `text-xs` (keep), the 'GMAIL' eyebrow is fine but lighten dividers to `border-white/[0.05]`. Collapse to at most two dividers; give each footer block `py-3` so the rhythm matches. Increase touch targets in the account row to min 36px height.

findings.title: No active/aria state polish on user dropdown trigger and sync controls
findings.current: The desktop Sync button and user dropdown trigger use only `transition-colors hover:bg-accent`; the dropdown trigger has no `aria-label`/expanded affordance beyond Radix defaults and no chevron. Sync shows text 'Syncing…' but the row doesn't otherwise indicate loading depth.
findings.problem: These are the two most-used affordances in the chrome yet they feel like plain text buttons. No press feedback, no clear 'this is a menu' affordance (no chevron), and the sync state change is just a spinning 12px icon — subtle to the point of being missable.
findings.recommendation: Add a small `ChevronsUpDown` (lucide) at the right of the user trigger at `text-muted-foreground/60`, and `whileTap={{ scale:0.98 }}`. On hover give the trigger `bg-accent/60` with 150ms ease. For sync, when `syncing`, also pulse the Gmail status dot or show a 2px top progress shimmer on the footer block so state is unmistakable.

findings.title: Page transition + AnimatePresence can flash because exit and enter overlap with mode='wait' but no min content height
findings.current: `<main class="... px-5 py-6 pb-24 md:pb-6">` wraps a `max-w-6xl space-y-6` column; `AnimatePresence mode='wait'` runs exit (150ms) then enter (150ms), ~300ms total, with the column having no min-height.
findings.problem: With `mode='wait'` the outgoing page fully unmounts before the new one mounts, so for ~150ms the content area is empty and the layout height collapses (no min-height), causing a visible vertical jump/flash especially between a tall Inbox and a short Settings. That undercuts the 'effortless' feel.
findings.recommendation: Either give the column `min-h-[calc(100vh-3rem)]` to hold height during the gap, or switch to a crossfade (`mode='popLayout'` / `mode='sync'`) with a 120ms exit and 220ms spring enter so frames overlap and there's no empty beat. Combined total under ~250ms keeps it snappy.

premiumOpportunities: Signature traveling selection: one shared `layoutId` highlight that glides between sidebar items on desktop AND between bottom-nav tabs on mobile, with a thin primary accent bar that springs vertically — a single, recognizable motion language for 'where am I' across both breakpoints.

Ambient security posture in the chrome: turn the Gmail footer status dot into a calm, breathing 'protected' pulse (slow 2.5s opacity 0.5→1 on bg-risk-safe). When a sync surfaces new high-risk mail, briefly tint the dot toward risk-quarantine and add a count badge on the Inbox nav item — reserving strong color for real risk per the design goal.

Command-style quick switcher: a Cmd/Ctrl-K palette overlay to jump between Dashboard/Inbox/Reports/Settings and trigger Sync, with spring-scale entrance (scale 0.96→1, blur-in). Makes the shell feel pro-grade and keyboard-first like Apple/Linear tools.

Frosted, depth-layered shell: give the sidebar and bottom nav matching `backdrop-blur-xl` translucency over a faint top-edge highlight so content visibly scrolls beneath the chrome — the 'deference + depth' that makes a UI feel premium rather than paneled.

Directional, hierarchy-aware page transitions: top-level tab switches crossfade in place, while drilling Inbox→EmailDetail slides forward (x+24) and Back slides back, so the spatial model of the app is felt, not just seen — all spring-based and reduced-motion safe.

Sync as a moment: replace the bare spinning icon with a subtle top-of-content shimmer/progress sweep and a settled toast ('Inbox up to date · 3 new scanned'), turning a background action into a confident, trustworthy beat.

findings.area: Dashboard page + StatCard + RiskDonut (first screen after login)
findings.currentStateSummary: The dashboard is a competent but generic admin layout: a row of 4 stat cards, then a 2/5 + 3/5 split of a Recharts donut ("Risk breakdown") and a "Needs your attention" quarantine list. It renders inside AppShell with no page title/header and no greeting — you land straight on a grid of cards, so there is zero "welcome / here is your security posture" framing. The risk palette is wired correctly via CSS vars (good), count-up and stagger animations exist (nice instinct), and empty/loading states are handled. But the surface reads as a metrics dashboard, not a calm security companion: four numeric KPIs of similar weight with no single hero verdict ("you are protected" / "N threats need action"), a small flat donut with a generic Recharts tooltip and no hover/interaction, and stat cards that are static rectangles with no tactile feedback. The data shown is also slightly off-target — it leans on raw counts (scanned/synced) rather than the one thing a security tool should answer first: am I safe right now, and what must I do.

findings.title: No hero verdict — four equal KPIs instead of one clear security answer
findings.current: The first thing after login is a 2x2 / 1x4 grid of four StatCards (Scanned, Likely phishing, Suspicious, Confirmed) all rendered at identical visual weight (text-2xl font-semibold, same card, same size). There is no page header, no greeting, no single summary statement.
findings.problem: Apple-grade dashboards lead with one clear answer, then progressively disclose detail (deference + clear hierarchy). A security tool's job is to answer 'am I safe?' in under a second. Here the user must read four numbers and mentally compute their status. 'Scanned' and 'synced' are operational telemetry, not a verdict — they are the least important numbers but occupy the first, primary-colored slot. Everything competing at the same weight means nothing leads.
findings.recommendation: Add a full-width hero 'posture' band above the KPIs (the lg:col-span-5 width). One line, large: when quarantined+suspicious === 0 show 'You're protected' in text-risk-safe with a subtle ShieldCheck, e.g. text-[28px]/tight font-semibold + a muted subline 'N messages scanned, nothing needs your attention'. When threats exist, show 'N messages need your attention' in text-risk-quarantine with a primary CTA to /inbox?riskBucket=quarantine. Demote Scanned/Synced to a single small caption inside the hero, not a top-left KPI card. Keep at most 3 KPI cards below, and make the threat-count cards visually heavier than the safe ones.

findings.title: Missing page header / greeting — you land in a grid with no orientation
findings.current: The connected return starts immediately with the stat-card grid. AppShell (components/layout/AppShell.jsx:37) wraps pages in space-y-6 with no per-page title. There is no <h1>, no 'Dashboard', no date, no account context.
findings.problem: Premium products establish context on entry (Apple's screens almost always name where you are and orient you). Jumping into a bare grid feels like a widget board, not a destination. There is also no <h1> on the page, which is an accessibility/landmark gap.
findings.recommendation:
Add a header block:

Security overview

with a muted subline showing the connected account email (account?.email) and 'Last synced {formatDateTime(lastSynced)}' moved up here from the attention card. Use space-y of 8 (32px) between header and content vs the current uniform 24px so the header breathes.

findings.title: Donut is small, flat, and inert — no hover lift, no active-slice focus, generic tooltip
findings.current: A 176px (h-44 w-44) Recharts donut, innerRadius 56 / outerRadius 80, paddingAngle 2, stroke none, with the default Recharts <Tooltip> styled via contentStyle. Center shows total + 'scanned'. No activeShape, no entrance animation control, no hover interaction between legend and slices.
findings.problem: This is the visual centerpiece of a security dashboard and currently looks like a default chart-library donut. No depth (Apple's 'depth' principle), no tactile response on hover, the stock Recharts tooltip has a hard-edged box and arrow that clashes with the rounded card system, and 176px is undersized for the hero data element. The legend (lines 60-71) and the chart don't talk to each other.
findings.recommendation: Enlarge to ~200-220px. Add activeIndex/activeShape so hovering a slice (or its legend row) expands it ~4px (outerRadius 80->84) with a soft drop using a subtle filter, and dims the others to ~0.4 opacity. Drive activeIndex from legend hover too (onMouseEnter on each <li>). Replace the stock Tooltip with a custom content component matching the card: bg var(--color-popover), rounded-lg, border var(--color-border), 8px padding, showing name + value + percentage. Add cornerRadius={4} to the Pie and animationDuration={700} with a custom easing. Center label should show the dominant verdict's share (e.g. '92% safe') not just a raw total — far more reassuring.

findings.title: Wrong data emphasis — center label says 'scanned', legend repeats raw counts; no percentages, no 'safe %'
findings.current: Center of donut: total scanned count + 'scanned'. Legend lists each verdict name with its raw integer value. donutData (DashboardPage.jsx:82-87) only includes safe/suspicious/likely/confirmed — it omits reviewed_safe and unscanned that the bucket system defines.
findings.problem: For a security overlay the emotionally relevant number is the safe percentage and the count that needs action, not a raw 'scanned' tally. Percentages are absent everywhere. Also the donut silently drops two of the six defined buckets (reviewed_safe, unscanned from lib/risk.js), so a user with many unscanned emails sees a chart that doesn't sum to their real inbox — quietly misleading for a trust tool.
findings.recommendation: Show '{safePct}%' large + 'safe' small in the center. Add a right-aligned percentage next to each legend value (e.g. 'Safe 142  ·  88%'). Either include an 'Unscanned' grey slice so the donut honestly reflects the whole inbox, or relabel the center 'of scanned' so it's truthful. Pull slice colors/labels from getRiskMeta() in lib/risk.js instead of hand-mapping var(--color-...) strings in DashboardPage so the donut can never drift from the single source of truth.

findings.title: StatCards have no hover/press feedback and are not interactive despite representing navigable buckets
findings.current: StatCard renders a motion.div with an entrance animation only (opacity/y on mount, duration 0.3). The Card itself has no whileHover, no whileTap, no cursor change, and is not a link — even though 'Likely phishing', 'Suspicious', 'Confirmed' map directly to inbox filters.
findings.problem: Tactile hover/press feedback is core to feeling 'premium' and 'alive'. These cards look clickable (icon, number, hint) but do nothing, which is a dead-end interaction. The number is the actionable hook to 'show me those emails' yet there's no affordance.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the threat StatCards in a Link to /inbox?riskBucket=<bucket>. Add whileHover={{ y: -2 }} and whileTap={{ scale: 0.98 }} with transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 400, damping: 30 }}, plus a hover border/glow: on hover bump border to the bucket color at ~30% and add a faint ring (e.g. ring-1 ring-<tone>/20). Add transition-colors and a subtle hover:bg-elevated. Show an ArrowRight that fades in on hover (opacity-0 group-hover:opacity-100).

findings.title: Stat number is undersized for a hero metric and the icon tile competes with it
findings.current: Value is text-2xl (24px) font-semibold; the colored icon tile is rounded-lg p-2.5 with an h-5 w-5 icon (~40px tile) sitting top-right at near-equal visual weight; label is text-xs uppercase tracking-wide.
findings.problem: On a real typographic scale the headline number should dominate the card. At 24px it is barely larger than surrounding UI, and the saturated soft-color icon tile pulls the eye away from the data (chrome competing with content — violates deference). Uppercase tracking-wide labels read as generic enterprise-analytics styling, not Apple-clean.
findings.recommendation: Raise the value to text-3xl/tabular-nums (30px) or text-4xl on lg, font-semibold, with a tighter leading-none. Shrink/quiet the icon: drop the soft background entirely or make it 28px with the tone color at lower opacity, so the number is unambiguously the focal point. Replace uppercase label with normal-case text-[13px] text-muted-foreground (Apple uses sentence case, not all-caps micro labels). Add tracking-tight to the number.

findings.title: Count-up animates on every sync re-render, including from a stale 0, and ignores prefers-reduced-motion
findings.current: useCountUp restarts whenever target changes (dep array [target, duration, delayMs]). Each syncVersion bump remounts the query and re-runs the count-up from 0. There is no prefers-reduced-motion guard; the easing is cubic-out over 600ms with a 60ms/card stagger.
findings.problem: Re-counting from 0 to 142 every time the user triggers a sync is gratuitous motion — Apple reserves motion for meaningful state change, not for re-displaying the same number. It also draws the eye away from whatever actually changed. No reduced-motion handling fails accessibility and feels less polished.
findings.recommendation: Only count up on first mount (or when the value actually changes by a meaningful delta), e.g. track a prevValue ref and animate from prev->next instead of 0->next. Guard with window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') — if reduced, setCount(target) immediately and skip rAF. Same guard should short-circuit the motion.div entrance and the donut animation.

findings.title: 'Needs your attention' list shows full EmailRow with a redundant RiskBadge — everything is the same bucket
findings.current: The attention card maps risky.slice(0,5) to <EmailRow> (components/inbox/EmailRow.jsx), which renders a left risk border AND a RiskBadge per row. Since riskyQuery is fixed to riskBucket:'quarantine', every row shows an identical 'Quarantine' badge and identical red left border.
findings.problem: Repeating the same badge five times is visual noise with zero information (a generic-admin tell). It also makes this list indistinguishable from the inbox. On a focused 'attention' panel each row should add signal — why is THIS one dangerous — not restate the bucket.
findings.recommendation: Use a slimmer dashboard-specific row (or pass a variant to EmailRow) that drops the redundant per-row badge and instead surfaces the top scan reason / score (e.g. 'Spoofed sender · link mismatch'). Keep one bucket color as a left accent only. Show sender + subject + the single strongest signal. This makes the panel earn its 'attention' title instead of mirroring the inbox.

findings.title: Donut and attention skeletons don't match their real layouts
findings.current: DashboardSkeleton renders the donut card as a single 176px circle skeleton with no legend placeholder, and the attention card as four h-12 rounded bars — but the real donut has a side legend and the real attention rows are 3-line email rows with a left border.
findings.problem: Layout shift between skeleton and content breaks the 'it just works' illusion. The eye anchors on the skeleton geometry, then content pops into a different shape. Apple-grade loading mirrors the final layout precisely so the transition is invisible.
findings.recommendation: Make the donut skeleton mirror the flex-row: circle on the left + 4 short legend-line skeletons on the right. Make the attention skeleton render rows that match EmailRow (left 3px accent strip, two text lines + a small badge pill), reusing the InboxSkeleton row shape. Also add a brief fade/crossfade (framer AnimatePresence or a 150ms opacity transition) when swapping skeleton->content instead of an instant cut.

findings.title: 'All clear' empty state in the attention card looks like an error/placeholder, not a reassuring success
findings.current: When risky.length===0 it shows <EmptyState icon={ShieldCheck} title='All clear' ...> with border-0. EmptyState (states.jsx:43-62) wraps the icon in a neutral bg-muted/60 grey circle with text-muted-foreground.
findings.problem: 'No threats' is the BEST possible outcome for a security tool and should feel good — calm green, a sense of resolution. Rendering it in dead grey (the same treatment as 'nothing scanned' / errors) squanders the single most reassuring moment in the product and reads as 'empty/missing data' rather than 'you're safe'.
findings.recommendation: Give the success-empty a dedicated treatment: ShieldCheck in text-risk-safe inside a bg-risk-safe-soft circle, title 'All clear' in foreground, subline 'No quarantined messages right now.' Optionally a one-time subtle spring scale-in on the shield (whileInView scale 0.9->1, spring stiffness 300). This is a great spot for a small signature 'protected' moment.

findings.title: Cards are uniformly flat (shadow-sm, single border) — no depth, layering, or translucency
findings.current: Every Card is 'rounded-xl border border-border bg-card shadow-sm'. The dashboard stacks many of these identical flat panels with uniform 16px (gap-4) gaps and no elevation differentiation.
findings.problem: Apple's 'depth' principle uses subtle layering and translucency to create hierarchy. Here all panels are the same flat plane, so the hero data (donut) doesn't feel more important than a stat card. shadow-sm on a #0a0d14 background is essentially invisible, so the only separation is a 1px #1f2838 border — flat and slightly austere.
findings.recommendation: Introduce two card elevations: keep flat for KPIs, and give the donut/attention cards a slightly lighter surface (bg-elevated #161d2b is already defined but unused here) plus a soft layered shadow (e.g. shadow-[0_1px_2px_rgba(0,0,0,0.4),0_8px_24px_-12px_rgba(0,0,0,0.5)]) and a 1px inner top highlight (ring-1 ring-white/5 or a subtle inset border-t-white/5) to catch light like macOS panels. Consider a very faint backdrop translucency on the hero band if anything sits behind it.

findings.title: Disconnected (no Gmail) state is a plain centered card, missing the chance for a premium first-run moment
findings.current: When !isConnected, returns a single Card with a small primary-tinted ShieldCheck tile, a heading, a paragraph, and a 'Connect Gmail' button. It's wrapped in an empty fragment with no entrance animation and no visual richness.
findings.problem: This is the literal first impression of the product for a new user, yet it's a tiny centered card on a dark void — generic onboarding, no sense of what they're about to get. No motion, no preview of value, no scale.
findings.recommendation: Make this a fuller hero: larger shield with a soft radial primary glow behind it (radial-gradient from var(--color-primary)/15 fading out), 3 quick value bullets (Sync · Scan · Verdict) with small icons, and the same spring entrance used elsewhere. Increase vertical rhythm (py-20+). This sets the premium tone before any data exists. Also note the redundant empty <></> fragment wrapper at lines 49/70 can be removed.

findings.title: Uniform gap-4 / no responsive type scaling — desktop feels cramped, no real typographic scale
findings.current: All grids use gap-4 (16px). The whole page is space-y-6 (24px from AppShell) at every breakpoint. Type sizes are flat: CardTitle text-base (16px), stat value text-2xl, labels text-xs — a compressed range.
findings.problem: Generous whitespace and a wide type scale are signatures of premium design. 16px gutters between large cards on a max-w-6xl desktop canvas feel dense, and a 12px->24px type range gives weak hierarchy. It reads efficient/utilitarian rather than confident and calm.
findings.recommendation: Scale spacing responsively: gap-4 on mobile, lg:gap-6 (24px) between cards; bump section spacing to lg:space-y-8. Widen the type scale: hero verdict ~28-32px, stat values 30px (lg:36px), section titles 18px (text-lg), captions 13px. Let the donut card have more internal padding (p-6/p-8) so the chart isn't edge-to-edge.

findings.title: Inconsistent muted text token: text-foreground/60 vs text-muted-foreground for the same role
findings.current: The label uses text-muted-foreground (#8a96aa) while the hint two lines down uses text-foreground/60 (a different computed grey). Both are 'secondary/quiet' text in the same card.
findings.problem: Two different greys for the same semantic role is exactly the kind of small inconsistency that separates polished from generic. It also undermines the design-token system the project explicitly set up (index.css comment says components should reference semantic names).
findings.recommendation: Standardize both quiet texts to text-muted-foreground. Reserve text-foreground/NN opacity tricks for genuinely distinct emphasis levels, and consider adding a --color-muted-foreground-subtle token if a third tier is truly needed.

premiumOpportunities: Signature 'posture ring' hero: replace the small breakdown donut with a large protection ring (gauge) that fills on load with spring physics and lands on the safe % — color shifts from amber->green as it settles when you're safe, or pulses gently at the quarantine color when threats exist. Center reads '94% safe' with a one-line status. This becomes the page's identity and instantly answers 'am I safe?'.

Interactive donut <-> legend linking: hovering a legend row expands the matching slice (outerRadius +4) and dims the rest; clicking a slice/legend deep-links to /inbox?riskBucket=<bucket>. Turns a static chart into a navigation surface and rewards exploration with tactile spring feedback.

'Threats need you' urgency band: when quarantine+suspicious > 0, show a calm-but-firm full-width band at top (border-l-risk-quarantine, soft tint) with the count and a single primary CTA — never a screaming red wall. When zero, it collapses into a quiet green 'You're protected' line. This is the calm-confidence security tone the brief asks for.

Animated number transitions on sync: instead of recounting from 0, animate stat values from previous->new with a subtle color flash on the cards that actually changed (e.g. a 600ms ring pulse in the bucket color), so a sync visibly communicates 'these 2 new threats appeared' rather than re-rendering everything.

Per-row threat reasoning in the attention list: each quarantined row shows its single strongest scan signal as a tiny chip ('SPF fail', 'lookalike domain', 'urgent language'), pulling from the existing scan data — gives the dashboard explanatory power (the 'XAI' in the product name) that no generic admin panel has.

Live sync shimmer: while a background sync runs (syncVersion changing), let the hero ring/donut show a subtle sweeping shimmer and the 'Last synced' label animate to 'Syncing…' with a soft pulse, then settle — making the app feel alive and trustworthy during the one operation users wait on.

findings.area: Inbox list + EmailRow + list grouping + skeletons
findings.currentStateSummary: The inbox is a single shadcn Card wrapping date-grouped rows, each row a Link with a 3px colored left border, a sender/date line, subject, snippet, and a soft RiskBadge pill on the right. Filter chips and a search box sit above the card; a numeric Pagination bar sits inside it. It is functional and reasonably clean, but it reads as a generic admin table, not a crafted Apple Mail / Linear list: rows have flat hover-only feedback (no press, no spring, no entrance animation despite Framer Motion being used elsewhere), risk is signaled twice (left bar + pill) yet weakly, the typographic hierarchy between sender/subject/snippet is nearly flat, density is loose and uniform, and the sticky group headers will not actually stick because the page scrolls at the document level. Several correctness/polish gaps exist too: redundant borders, an unread concept that does not exist, filter chips that omit two risk buckets, and skeletons that do not match real row geometry.

findings.title: Sticky date-group headers will not stick — wrong scroll container
findings.current: Group headers use `sticky top-0 z-10 ... bg-card/95 backdrop-blur`. But AppShell's `<main>` (components/layout/AppShell.jsx:36) has no overflow; the document/body scrolls. The headers' sticky ancestor is effectively the viewport, and `top-0` sits under nothing — there is no app top bar offset, and the Card is not a scroll container, so the sticky behaviour is either a no-op or visually broken depending on viewport offset.
findings.problem: A signature feature of Apple Mail / iOS lists is the section header that pins and pushes the previous one as you scroll. Here it is dead code that adds a `backdrop-blur` cost for no payoff, and the headers scroll away like normal content. It reads as half-implemented.
findings.recommendation: Decide the scroll model. Simplest premium fix: keep document scroll but make headers genuinely useful by giving them a real pinned offset — wrap headers in `sticky top-2 z-20` AND ensure the Card does not clip (`overflow-hidden` on the Card at line 161 will prevent sticky from working — remove it or move it). Better: render the header pill style as `bg-background/80 backdrop-blur-md` with a 1px hairline only on its bottom edge (`shadow-[0_1px_0_var(--color-border)]`) so it floats over rows. Verify with a >10 row page that the previous header is replaced by the next, iOS-style.

findings.title: Rows have no entrance, stagger, or press feedback — list feels static
findings.current: Each row is a plain `<Link>` with only `transition-colors hover:bg-accent/50`. No mount animation, no stagger, no active/press state. Meanwhile StatCard (components/dashboard/StatCard.jsx:44) and VerdictBanner already use Framer Motion with `y:10 → 0` + 60ms stagger.
findings.problem: The inbox is where users spend most time, yet it is the least alive surface. Pages fade in via PageTransition but the rows arrive flat and identical. There is no tactile confirmation when tapping a row (critical on mobile, where BottomNav implies heavy mobile use). Apple-grade lists settle in with a brief, physical stagger and depress slightly on press.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the row in `motion(Link)`. Entrance: `initial={{opacity:0, y:6}} animate={{opacity:1, y:0}}` with `transition={{duration:0.22, ease:[0.22,1,0.36,1], delay: Math.min(index*0.025, 0.2)}}` (cap the stagger so page-9 rows are not slow). Press: `whileTap={{ scale: 0.992 }}` and a spring `{type:'spring', stiffness:400, damping:30}`. Pass an `index` prop from InboxPage's `.map`. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (Framer's `useReducedMotion`) to disable y/stagger.

findings.title: Risk is signaled twice but weakly; the left bar is a thin afterthought
findings.current: Risk is shown by a `3px solid` colored left border (inline style) AND a soft RiskBadge pill on the right. The safe/reviewed_safe states both render a full-saturation green bar + pill, so a 90%-safe inbox is a wall of green-and-red stripes competing for attention.
findings.problem: For a security tool the brief is 'calm confidence, reserve strong color for real risk.' Currently every single row screams a color, which trains users to ignore color — the opposite of what you want. The 3px bar is also too thin to scan and too saturated for safe mail. Apple would make the default (safe) recede and let only quarantine/phishing/needs_review draw the eye.
findings.recommendation: Make safe/reviewed_safe/unscanned visually quiet: no left bar (or a 2px bar at ~20% opacity), and a borderless/no-fill badge or just a small dot. Reserve the colored left accent and soft-filled badge for needs_review/quarantine/confirmed_phishing only. Widen the risk accent for those to a 3px bar PLUS a faint full-row tint for quarantine/phishing using the existing `bg-risk-quarantine-soft`/`bg-risk-phishing-soft` at low alpha (e.g. `bg-risk-quarantine-soft/40`). Drive this from a single helper in lib/risk.js (e.g. `tone.emphasis: 'quiet' | 'loud'`) so it stays the single source of truth.

findings.title: Flat typographic hierarchy — sender, subject, snippet nearly indistinguishable
findings.current: Sender is `text-sm font-medium`, subject is `text-sm text-foreground/90`, snippet is `text-xs text-muted-foreground`. Sender and subject are the same size and weight; only a 10% opacity separates them. Date is `text-xs text-muted-foreground`.
findings.problem: In a scannable mail list the eye should land on sender, then subject, in one beat. Here sender and subject blur together (same 14px), so each row demands reading rather than scanning. There is no real typographic scale — the whole row lives in 12–14px. Apple Mail uses a clear size+weight step between sender (bold) and preview (regular, dimmer).
findings.recommendation: Establish a 3-step scale: sender `text-[15px] font-semibold text-foreground tracking-[-0.01em]`; subject `text-sm font-normal text-foreground/75`; snippet `text-[13px] text-muted-foreground`. Make the date `text-xs tabular-nums text-muted-foreground/80` and right-align it on its own baseline with the sender. Consider merging subject+snippet into one line on dense view to reduce row height, with subject in foreground and snippet dimmed inline (` — `).

findings.title: Filter chips omit two risk buckets and the active state is unconvincing
findings.current: RISK_FILTERS (lib/risk.js:110) only exposes All, Quarantine, Suspicious, Confirmed phishing, Safe — `reviewed_safe` and `unscanned` rows can exist but have no filter. Active chip is `border-primary bg-primary/15 text-primary`; inactive is muted. Counts come from a separate monthly-summary query and read `(n)` in 70%-opacity parens.
findings.problem: Users cannot filter to the buckets the app itself defines, and an inbox full of `unscanned` mail has no way to be surfaced. Visually the chips are generic pills with no risk color — the Quarantine chip looks identical to the Safe chip, missing an obvious chance to color-code the filter by its own risk hue and reinforce the palette. The blue active state collides with the brand color used everywhere else.
findings.recommendation: Add `unscanned` (and optionally fold `reviewed_safe` into Safe via backend or a combined filter). Color each chip by its risk tone when active: e.g. Quarantine active = `bg-risk-quarantine-soft text-risk-quarantine border-risk-quarantine/40`, Safe active = risk-safe tones, All active = primary. Show the count as a pill-within-pill (`rounded-full bg-foreground/10 px-1.5 text-[10px]`) rather than dim parens. Animate the active pill with a Framer `layoutId='filterPill'` sliding indicator for an Apple segmented-control feel.

findings.title: Skeleton geometry does not match real rows — visible layout shift on load
findings.current: InboxSkeleton renders flat rows with `border-left: 3px solid transparent` and three skeleton lines, but it omits the date-group headers entirely and uses fixed widths (`w-32`, `w-56`, `w-40`). Real rows are grouped under sticky headers and the badge is `h-5 w-16`. So the skeleton card has a different vertical rhythm than the loaded card.
findings.problem: The whole point of a skeleton is zero perceived layout shift. Because the skeleton lacks the 'Today/Yesterday' header bands and the row paddings differ subtly, the content visibly jumps and reflows when data arrives — the opposite of the calm, instant feel Apple targets. Fixed widths also make every skeleton row identical, which reads as obviously fake.
findings.recommendation: Mirror the real structure: include 1–2 faux group-header bands (`h-3 w-16` in a `px-4 py-1.5` strip) and vary line widths per row (cycle widths so rows look organic). Match exact paddings/heights to EmailRow. Replace the `animate-pulse` (states.jsx via skeleton.jsx:6) with a left-to-right shimmer sweep (`bg-gradient-to-r` + `bg-[length:200%_100%]` keyframe over ~1.4s) for a more premium loading texture than a uniform opacity pulse.

findings.title: Redundant row borders — inline left border + class bottom border + divider
findings.current: EmailRow sets an inline `borderLeft: 3px solid tone.hex` AND className `border-b border-border/60 ... last:border-b-0`, while the parent in InboxPage.jsx:169 ALSO wraps rows in `divide-y divide-border/60`. So separators are declared twice (border-b + divide-y) and can double up / fight at group boundaries.
findings.problem: Double-declared borders are a code smell that produces inconsistent 1px/2px hairlines and makes the list look slightly dirty under close inspection — exactly the kind of imprecision an Apple-grade list never has. It also means changing the divider color requires editing two places.
findings.recommendation: Pick one separator owner. Keep `divide-y divide-border/40` on the group container in InboxPage and REMOVE `border-b border-border/60 last:border-b-0` from EmailRow. Soften the divider to `/40` (currently /60 is heavy for a dense list). Keep only the risk left border as inline (and gate it per the risk-emphasis finding).

findings.title: No unread / read distinction — every row weighted identically
findings.current: Rows render sender always at `font-medium` regardless of read state. There is no isRead/seen treatment, no unread dot, no weight or background difference.
findings.problem: Even though this is a security overlay rather than a full client, 'have I looked at this flagged message yet?' is the core user question. Apple Mail's most basic affordance — bold unread + blue dot — is absent, so the list gives no sense of progress through one's risk triage. The list feels like a static report, not a working queue.
findings.recommendation: If the backend exposes a read/reviewed flag (the riskBucket `reviewed_safe`/`confirmed_phishing` already imply user action), render reviewed rows dimmer (`opacity-70` / sender `font-normal`) and un-actioned risk rows bolder, with a small leading 6px unread dot in the risk tone for un-reviewed quarantine/needs_review. If no read flag exists, at minimum dim `reviewed_safe`/`confirmed_phishing` rows so the eye is pulled to outstanding `quarantine`/`needs_review` items.

findings.title: No sender avatar / monogram — rows lack an anchor and scan rhythm
findings.current: Rows start directly with text; there is no leading visual element except the thin colored border. getSenderName/getSenderAddress exist in lib/email.js but only the name string is used.
findings.problem: Every premium mail/list UI (Apple Mail, Gmail, Linear, Things) uses a leading avatar/monogram circle to give each row a fixed-width anchor, create a vertical scan column, and add color/personality. Without it, rows are a left-ragged block of text and the 3px bar is the only leading element — visually thin and monotonous.
findings.recommendation: Add a 36px circular monogram on the left: initials from getSenderName, background derived from a deterministic hash of getSenderAddress (mapped to a small palette, or a neutral `bg-muted` with `text-muted-foreground`). For risk rows, optionally ring the avatar in the risk tone (`ring-2 ring-risk-quarantine/50`) — this lets you drop the separate left bar AND badge for a cleaner, more iconic row. This becomes the row's tactile anchor and dramatically improves scannability.

findings.title: Loose, uniform density — no rhythm, wasteful on desktop
findings.current: Every row is `px-4 py-3` (12px vertical) with three stacked lines (sender, subject, snippet), giving ~72px+ rows. Group header is `px-4 py-1.5`. PAGE_SIZE is 10 (InboxPage.jsx:21).
findings.problem: Three full-size lines per row + 10 rows + pagination means a lot of scrolling for little content, and the rhythm is monotone — no breathing difference between groups, no comfortable/compact option. Apple lists feel tighter and more rhythmic; here the snippet line bloats height without adding much (it is often redundant with subject).
findings.recommendation: Tighten to a 2-line default (sender+date on line 1, subject with inline dimmed snippet on line 2) at `px-4 py-2.5`, yielding ~56px rows. Add slightly more top padding to the FIRST row of each group (`pt-3`) for rhythm. Increase PAGE_SIZE to 15–20 to reduce pagination friction, or move toward infinite scroll (see opportunities). Add a comfortable/compact density toggle persisted in localStorage if you want a signature pro touch.

findings.title: Search input lacks clear button, loading/affordance, and keyboard shortcut
findings.current: Search is a plain Input with a left magnifier icon, 300ms debounce. No clear (x) button, no visible 'searching…' state while the debounce/fetch is in flight, no '/' or Cmd+K focus shortcut, and the search row is detached from the list card.
findings.problem: Apple/Linear search feels instant and reversible: you can clear in one tap and you always know whether results are live. Here, after typing, there is a 300ms+network gap with no feedback (the whole list flips to InboxSkeleton, which is jarring for a search refine), and clearing means manually selecting and deleting text.
findings.recommendation: Add a trailing clear button (`X`, appears when searchInput) that resets q and page. Show a subtle inline spinner in the input (replace the magnifier with Loader2) while `searchInput !== debouncedSearch || loading`. Add a `/` global shortcut to focus, with a faint `⌘K`/`/` hint chip at the input's right. During search refinement, keep the existing list dimmed (`opacity-50 pointer-events-none`) instead of swapping to the full skeleton, so results refine in place.

findings.title: Pagination is a numbered desktop control, mismatched to a mobile-first list
findings.current: Pagination renders numbered page buttons (h-7 w-7) with prev/next chevrons and ellipses, inside the card footer. The app has a BottomNav and MobileSync FAB (AppShell.jsx) implying heavy mobile use.
findings.problem: Numbered pagination is a web-table pattern; it feels clerical, not 'effortless,' and the 28px tap targets fail the 44px iOS minimum. On a triage list users want continuous flow, not page-hopping. The control also lives inside `Card overflow-hidden`, which combined with sticky headers fights the layout.
findings.recommendation: For premium feel, replace numbered pagination with infinite scroll / 'Load more' using an IntersectionObserver sentinel that appends the next page (keep `normalizeEmailList` + pagination.totalPages to know when to stop). If keeping pages, enlarge controls to `h-9 min-w-9` (44px touch on mobile), make prev/next the primary action with page count as quiet text, and animate page changes with a short cross-fade so the list does not hard-cut.

findings.title: Filter chip / search bar disconnected from the list card
findings.current: Filter chips + search sit in a free-floating flex row above the Card; the AppShell adds `space-y-6` between siblings, so there is a 24px gap and no visual containment relationship.
findings.problem: The controls read as unrelated to the list they drive. Premium lists (Linear, Apple Mail) bind the toolbar to the list as one cohesive surface — a single elevated panel with a divided toolbar — so the eye understands 'these controls filter this content.' The current floating chips look like a generic filter bar bolted on.
findings.recommendation: Pull the toolbar into the top of the same Card as a sticky toolbar header (`sticky top-0` toolbar row with a bottom hairline), so filters + search + list are one panel. Reduce the gap (`space-y-3`). This also gives a natural home for a result count and a sync/refresh affordance, and reinforces the depth principle (one elevated, layered surface).

findings.title: Hover feedback is color-only and slightly too strong; no cursor/elevation cue
findings.current: Hover is `hover:bg-accent/50` (accent #1c2740 at 50%) with `transition-colors` (default 150ms). No duration tuning, no subtle inset/elevation, no chevron reveal.
findings.problem: `bg-accent/50` is a fairly heavy blue wash that fights the risk colors and feels like a table-row highlight rather than a soft, premium hover. There is no sense the row is a tappable card — no depth, no directional affordance toward the detail view it navigates to.
findings.recommendation: Soften hover to `hover:bg-foreground/[0.03]` (neutral, not brand-blue) with `transition-[background-color,transform] duration-150 ease-out`. On hover, fade in a trailing `ChevronRight` (opacity 0→60%, translateX 0→2px) to signal navigation, and add `active:scale-[0.995]`. Keep the risk tint underneath untouched so hover layers over it rather than replacing it.

findings.title: Card has overflow-hidden — clips focus rings and breaks sticky
findings.current: The list Card uses `overflow-hidden` to clip the rounded corners of grouped content and pagination.
findings.problem: `overflow-hidden` on the scroll/sticky ancestor prevents `position: sticky` group headers from working and clips keyboard focus rings on the first/last rows (accessibility regression for keyboard users tabbing the list). It is a quiet correctness issue masked by the fact that sticky is already broken.
findings.recommendation: Remove `overflow-hidden` from the Card and instead round the inner edges (`first:rounded-t-xl`/`last:rounded-b-xl` on group wrappers, or `rounded-xl` on the Card with `overflow-clip` only where strictly needed). Ensure `:focus-visible` rings on EmailRow render fully (add `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-inset` to the Link, since Links currently have no visible focus style at all — a real a11y gap).

findings.title: EmailRow Link has no focus-visible style and badge text duplicates the bar meaning
findings.current: The row `<Link>` has no `focus-visible` ring class. RiskBadge (size sm) shows a text label like 'Phishing'/'Suspicious' for every row, alongside the colored left bar.
findings.problem: Keyboard and screen-reader users get no focus indicator on the primary list action — a hard accessibility failure for the most-used surface. Separately, repeating the risk word on every row is noisy redundancy with the left bar/tint; Apple would rely on color+icon for the common case and reserve words for emphasis.
findings.recommendation: Add `outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-inset rounded-sm` to the Link. Give the row an `aria-label` like `${sender}: ${subject}, risk ${label}` so the badge can become icon-only (or a dot) for safe rows without losing SR meaning. Keep the full worded badge only for quarantine/confirmed_phishing where the explicit word adds urgency.

findings.title: Group label set is hardcoded and date logic is duplicated
findings.current: DATE_GROUP_ORDER = ['Today','Yesterday','This week','Older'] is hardcoded in the page and must stay in sync with getDateGroupLabel (utils/formatDate.js:42). formatEmailDate (line 14) re-implements the same start-of-today/week math independently.
findings.problem: Two copies of week-boundary math will drift (one already differs subtly in style), and 'Older' is a coarse bucket — a 6-month-old inbox collapses everything beyond this week into one undifferentiated pile, hurting scannability. Not Apple-grade temporal grouping.
findings.recommendation: Centralize grouping: export an ordered `DATE_GROUPS` and a single `groupKey(date)` from formatDate.js, and have getDateGroupLabel/formatEmailDate share the boundary helpers. Expand buckets to 'Today / Yesterday / This week / Last week / This month / Earlier' (or month names for Older) so long lists stay navigable. Keep these as the single source so labels and ordering can never diverge.

findings.title: Filter count mapping is fragile and can mislabel counts
findings.current: FILTER_COUNT_MAP maps chip keys to monthly-summary count fields ('' → syncedEmails, quarantine → quarantined, needs_review → suspicious, confirmed_phishing → markedPhishing, safe → safe). Counts come from a separate `getMonthlySummary()` query while the list comes from `getEmails()`.
findings.problem: The chip counts reflect a MONTHLY summary, but the list reflects the full (paged) dataset for the current search. So a chip can read '(3)' while the filtered list shows 12, or vice versa — the numbers and the content disagree, which erodes trust in a security tool. There is also no count for the 'All' set matching the current search.
findings.recommendation: Source chip counts from the same query/scope as the list (ideally a `counts` block returned by the emails endpoint honoring the active search), or clearly scope the chips to 'this month'. At minimum, hide counts when a search `q` is active (they cannot be correct). Ensure parity so the badge number always equals what the user will see when they click.

premiumOpportunities: Signature triage flow: turn the list into a working queue, not a report. Sort/raise un-actioned quarantine + needs_review to the top with a subtle pinned 'Needs your attention (n)' band, and when a row is reviewed, animate it settling/dimming in place (Framer layout animation) so the user feels progress. This is the one interaction that would make SecureInbox feel purpose-built rather than a generic mail list.

Swipe-to-act on mobile (iOS Mail muscle memory): swipe a row left to reveal 'Mark phishing', right to reveal 'Mark safe', backed by the existing ReviewActions, with spring snap and color reveal in the row's risk tone. Pairs perfectly with the existing BottomNav mobile-first shell.

Infinite scroll with an IntersectionObserver sentinel and a thin top progress hairline, replacing numbered pagination — append pages seamlessly so triage is one continuous, momentum-scrolled surface. Keep sticky iOS-style section headers that pin and shove as you scroll.

Quick-look hover/long-press preview: hovering a row (desktop) or long-pressing (mobile) pops a small spring-scaled card with the verdict reason + key risk signals, so users can triage without opening the full detail page. Reuses VerdictBanner content.

Command-palette / type-ahead search (⌘K) that filters by sender, subject, and risk bucket with inline highlighted matches in the rows, plus an animated segmented-control filter (Framer `layoutId` sliding pill) — gives the list the crisp, keyboard-driven feel of Linear.

Calm risk choreography: when scans complete after a sync, animate newly-flagged rows with a one-time soft pulse of their risk tone (single 600ms breathe, then settle), drawing the eye to new threats exactly once instead of a permanent wall of color — embodies 'reserve strong color for real risk.'

Deterministic colored sender monograms as the row anchor, with a risk-tone ring for flagged senders — replaces both the thin left bar and the worded badge for a cleaner, more iconic, instantly-scannable row column.

findings.currentStateSummary: The reading view is a clean, functional two-column layout (message left, sticky security panel right) stacked under a verdict banner and a subject/sender/date header block. It reuses generic Card/Button primitives and the global PageTransition (opacity + y:6, 150ms easeOut) for "open" — there is no email-specific scaling or focus animation, so opening a message feels like any other route change. The email HTML body is sanitized correctly and rendered inside a bordered, slightly-tinted container, but the `email-body` class it relies on has NO backing CSS rules (only a handful of inline Tailwind arbitrary-variant selectors), so real-world email markup (headings, lists, blockquotes, tables, spacing) renders with browser defaults and no typographic control. Prev/next exists only as two small ghost icon buttons with no keyboard support, no position indicator (e.g. "3 of 24"), and no transition between messages. Overall it reads as a tidy dashboard panel rather than a focused, elegant "reading room."

findings.title: email-body class has no backing CSS — email typography is unstyled browser defaults
findings.current:
The body div uses className="email-body ... [&_a]:text-primary [&_a]:underline [&_img]:max-w-full [&_table]:max-w-full ...". A grep shows `email-body` appears ONLY in this file — there are zero `.email-body` rules in index.css. So headings (h1-h3),
    /
      ,
      ,

      spacing,

      , padding all fall back to UA defaults inside a dark theme: black-on-dark text from inline email styles can become invisible, list bullets vanish, heading sizes are random.
findings.problem: Real emails are HTML-heavy. Without a scoped typographic reset/stylesheet the single most-viewed content in the app renders inconsistently and sometimes illegibly — the opposite of Apple-grade clarity. The inline arbitrary variants only patch links/images/tables, not the prose itself.
findings.recommendation: Add a real scoped stylesheet under @layer components in index.css, e.g. `.email-body { color: var(--color-foreground); font-size: 0.9375rem; line-height: 1.65; }` plus `.email-body :where(h1,h2,h3){font-weight:600;line-height:1.3;margin:1.25em 0 0.5em} .email-body :where(p,ul,ol){margin:0 0 0.85em} .email-body :where(ul,ol){padding-left:1.4em} .email-body li{margin:0.25em 0} .email-body blockquote{border-left:3px solid var(--color-border);padding-left:1rem;color:var(--color-muted-foreground);margin:0.85em 0} .email-body hr{border-color:var(--color-border);margin:1.5em 0} .email-body a{color:var(--color-primary)} .email-body img{border-radius:8px}`. This guarantees legible, consistent prose regardless of the sender's markup.

findings.title: No keyboard navigation for prev/next or back — fails a focused reader's mental model
findings.current: Prev/next is only reachable by clicking two 32px ghost icon buttons (h-8 w-8). There is no window keydown listener: j/k, ArrowLeft/ArrowRight, or Esc-to-go-back do nothing.
findings.problem: Apple-grade reading surfaces (Mail.app, Things, Linear) are keyboard-first. A security reviewer triaging an inbox wants to flick through messages without reaching for the mouse. Absence of this makes the surface feel like a web form, not a tool.
findings.recommendation: Add a useEffect keydown listener: ArrowLeft/'k' → navTo(prevId), ArrowRight/'j' → navTo(nextId), 'Escape' → navigate(-1) (guard against typing in inputs via e.target.tagName check). Surface the shortcuts in the button title attrs ('Previous (←)'). ~15 lines, no new deps.

findings.title: Generic PageTransition is the only 'open' animation — no focused, tactile reveal
findings.current: Opening an email reuses the app-wide PageTransition: opacity 0→1, y 6→0, duration 0.15s, ease 'easeOut'. The VerdictBanner separately fades in (y:-4, 200ms easeOut). Nothing scales, and the message card has no distinct entrance.
findings.problem: The brief asks for purposeful spring-physics motion and a reading experience that feels like the content comes forward into focus. A flat 150ms tween shared with every route makes opening a message feel incidental, not like entering a focused reading mode. Linear/Apple Mail subtly scale + settle the detail content.
findings.recommendation: Give the detail page its own entrance using a spring: wrap the header+columns in a motion.div with initial={{opacity:0, y:8, scale:0.985}} animate={{opacity:1, y:0, scale:1}} transition={{type:'spring', stiffness:380, damping:34, mass:0.9}}. Optionally stagger: verdict banner first (delay:0), header (delay:0.04), body card (delay:0.08). Keep total under ~350ms.

findings.title: Switching prev/next has no transition — content swaps instantly with stale flash
findings.file: frontend/src/pages/EmailDetailPage.jsx:60,77-79 (load() sets loading, navTo changes route param)
findings.current: navTo changes the :emailId param; the page is keyed by location.pathname in AppShell so PageTransition re-runs, but `if (loading && !email) return <LoadingState>` only shows the spinner on first load — on prev/next the OLD email stays on screen while the new one fetches, then snaps in. There is no directional motion reflecting prev vs next.
findings.problem: Flicking through messages feels janky: old subject/body lingers, then jumps. A premium reader gives a quick directional slide (left-going vs right-going) so the user feels which direction they moved.
