findings.recommendation: Wrap the message column in AnimatePresence mode='popLayout' keyed by paramId, with custom direction (track whether prev or next was pressed). Use x: ±16 → 0 with the same spring. While the next email loads, dim the body to opacity-50 + pointer-events-none rather than leaving it fully interactive with stale data.

findings.title: Subject/sender hierarchy is too flat for a reading view
findings.current: Subject is h1 text-xl (20px) font-semibold; the sender line is one cramped flex-wrap row at text-sm (14px) mixing senderName (foreground/90), <address> (muted), a '·' separator (text-border), and the full datetime (muted) — all same size, all on one line.
findings.problem: 20px is small for the single most important line on a reading surface, and packing name+address+date into one same-weight row gives no clear sender identity. Apple HIG wants a strong, calm hierarchy: who → subject → when, with breathing room. No sender avatar/monogram means the 'from' has no visual anchor — important for phishing where impersonation matters.
findings.recommendation: Bump subject to text-2xl (24px)/font-semibold/leading-tight/tracking-tight. Add a 36-40px circular monogram avatar (first letter of senderName, bg derived from a hash) to the left of the sender block. Put senderName at text-sm font-medium foreground on line 1, address at text-xs muted on the same line, and move the date to its own muted text-xs line or right-align it. Increase pb-4 to pb-5 and gap to space-y-2.

findings.title: Email body container reads as a nested 'inset box' rather than a clean reading surface
findings.current: Body lives in Card > CardContent(pt-5) > a second div with `overflow-x-auto rounded-lg border border-border/60 bg-background/40 p-4`. So there are two stacked containers (card border + inner border) and a darker tint (background/40) behind the message.
findings.problem: Double-bordered, double-tinted nesting is visual noise and fights 'deference — content first, chrome recedes.' Tinting the reading area darker than the card pushes the actual email backward and reduces contrast on dark-on-dark email markup.
findings.recommendation: Drop the inner border + bg-background/40; let the email body sit directly on the card surface with comfortable padding (px-6 py-5). Keep overflow-x-auto only for wide tables. If a visual boundary is wanted, use a single hairline at the top (border-t border-border/50) rather than a full inset box. Consider a max reading width (e.g. max-w-[680px] mx-auto) for long text emails so line length stays comfortable.

findings.title: Verdict banner is visually identical in weight for safe and confirmed-phishing
findings.current: Every verdict uses the same chrome: rounded-xl, px-4 py-3, a 16px (h-4 w-4) icon, soft tinted bg + 30%-opacity colored border. Only the hue changes between safe/suspicious/quarantine/phishing.
findings.problem: The brief explicitly says reserve strong color for real risk and project calm confidence. Right now a safe email shouts as loudly as confirmed phishing (same border weight, same fill). There's no escalation in visual urgency, so the banner neither reassures on safe nor commands attention on phishing.
findings.recommendation: Make the banner tiered. Safe/reviewed_safe: minimal — no fill, just a small colored check + 'Safe' in muted weight (let it recede). Suspicious/quarantine/phishing: keep the soft fill, increase icon to h-5 w-5, add a subtle left accent (border-l-2) using the risk token, and a single calm pulse on mount for quarantine/phishing only (scale 1→1.015 spring, once). Never animate the safe state. This uses the existing risk tokens, no new colors.

findings.title: Prev/next gives no position context and the controls are tiny
findings.current: Two h-8 w-8 ghost chevron buttons, shown only if prevId||nextId. No '3 of 24' indicator. If the user lands via deep link (no location.state.ids), the whole nav block disappears with no explanation.
findings.problem: Reaching the edge of the list (disabled button) or arriving with no list context is silent and confusing. A premium reader always tells you where you are. The 32px hit targets are also below the comfortable 40px tap target on the surface meant for fast triage.
findings.recommendation: Add a centered muted indicator between the chevrons: `{currentIdx+1} / {ids.length}`, shown when ids.length>0. Bump buttons to h-9 w-9. When there is no ids context (deep link), keep a single 'Back to inbox' Link instead of hiding navigation entirely.

findings.title: Mixed icon button sizing and overridden defaults signal inconsistent system
findings.file: frontend/src/pages/EmailDetailPage.jsx:100-118 (size="icon" then className="h-8 w-8"); button.jsx:26 icon default is h-10 w-10
findings.current: size='icon' yields h-10 w-10 from buttonVariants, but the prev/next buttons override to h-8 w-8 inline. The re-scan button is a full-width ghost at text-xs, while Back is size='sm'. Three different button scales coexist in the header/panel.
findings.problem: Overriding the design-system size inline is the kind of one-off that erodes consistency — an Apple-grade UI has a deliberate, repeated control rhythm. The default 'icon' size existing but being overridden suggests the size scale doesn't fit this surface.
findings.recommendation: Standardize: use a single small icon size (add an `icon-sm` -> h-9 w-9 variant to button.jsx) and use it for prev/next instead of inline overrides. Align Back and prev/next to the same height (h-9). Keep the re-scan action visually subordinate but not a different text size — text-sm muted is enough.

findings.title: Re-scan control is buried and gives weak feedback
findings.current: Re-scan is a full-width ghost button at text-xs, sandwiched between the review card and the collapsible scan details. On click it sets rescanning, spins a 14px loader, and calls load() which re-fetches everything; there's no toast and the verdict banner just silently changes when done.
findings.problem: Re-running the security scan is a meaningful action on a security tool, but it's styled like a tertiary footnote and the result change isn't celebrated or acknowledged. The user can't tell the scan actually re-ran if the verdict is unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Move re-scan to a clearly labeled secondary action at the top of the security panel (or as an icon-button beside the 'Scan details' heading). On success fire a Sonner toast ('Re-scan complete — verdict unchanged' / 'Verdict updated to X') and let the VerdictBanner animate its change (key it by riskBucket so AnimatePresence runs). Disable + spinner is fine, but pair it with a result confirmation.

findings.title: Remote images load with no privacy gate — security-tool inconsistency
findings.current: DOMPurify strips scripts/iframes/forms but keeps with remote src; the JSDoc even notes 'Remote images are kept'. So opening a quarantine/phishing email immediately pings the attacker's tracking pixels.
findings.problem: For a phishing-detection product this is both a trust and a UX gap: serious mail clients block remote content by default and offer 'Load images'. Auto-loading remote images on a likely-phishing message undermines the product's whole premise.
findings.recommendation: For needs_review/quarantine/confirmed_phishing buckets, rewrite img src to data-src in the sanitizer (or strip and count them), and render a calm inline banner in EmailBody: 'Remote images blocked to protect your privacy — Load images' (a button that restores src). For safe buckets you may auto-load. This is a signature trust moment unique to this product.

findings.title: Plain-text fallback uses a <pre> with no max width — long URLs/quotes break the column
findings.current: Text bodies render in `<pre className="whitespace-pre-wrap break-words font-sans text-sm leading-relaxed text-foreground/90">`. No max reading width, slightly muted (foreground/90), 14px.
findings.problem: whitespace-pre-wrap preserves source line breaks, so machine-wrapped plain-text emails get ragged double-wrapping; full-width lines on a wide lg column hurt readability (ideal ~66ch). foreground/90 for body copy is slightly low-contrast for the primary content.
findings.recommendation: Use full `text-foreground` and bump to text-[0.9375rem]/leading-[1.65]; cap width with max-w-[68ch]. Keep whitespace-pre-wrap but the same .email-body prose rules should apply so HTML and text fallbacks feel like one reading experience.

findings.title: Sticky security panel can overpower the message on tall viewports
findings.current: Grid is lg:grid-cols-3 with message at col-span-2 and the security panel taking the full third column, sticky top-4 with its own scroll. The panel holds: review card, re-scan, and an expanded-by-default ScanDetails (AI explanation + score bars + rules).
findings.problem: With scanExpanded defaulting to true (line 36), the security column is very tall and visually dense, competing with the email for attention. On a security overlay the content should still lead; right now the chrome (analysis) can dominate the reading column.
findings.recommendation: Keep the verdict + your-review visible, but collapse ScanDetails by default (scanExpanded=false) so the reader chooses to dig in. Consider narrowing the panel (message col-span-2 of a 5-col grid → roughly 60/40) and reducing inter-card gap from space-y-4 to space-y-3 so the panel feels like one cohesive sidebar, not four stacked cards.

findings.title: Date format is verbose and inconsistent with the inbox
findings.current: Detail view shows full 'Jun 05, 2026, 02:30 PM' via formatDateTime, while the inbox list uses the relative formatEmailDate ('Yesterday', 'Mon', '14:30').
findings.problem: The absolute string is fine but the day has a leading zero ('05') and the comma-heavy Intl output reads bureaucratic; it also doesn't match the friendlier inbox formatting, a small consistency seam.
findings.recommendation: Show a relative-but-precise line: primary 'Yesterday at 14:30' (reuse formatEmailDate logic) with the full timestamp available on hover via title. Drop the day-of-month leading zero (day:'numeric'). Keep absolute precision accessible since exact send time matters for phishing forensics.

premiumOpportunities: Signature 'Load images' privacy gate tied to the risk verdict: remote content is blocked for suspicious/quarantine/phishing emails by default, with a single calm inline 'Load images' affordance. This is a genuine wow moment unique to a phishing tool — the product visibly protects you the instant you open a risky message, not just labels it.

Inline link risk highlighting inside the body: since the scanner already extracts links, decorate <a> tags in the rendered email whose href domain mismatches the visible text or matches a triggered rule with a subtle risk underline + a hover popover showing the true destination. Reading the email itself becomes the explanation, fusing content and verdict (true explainable-AI feel).

Keyboard-first reading mode: j/k or ←/→ to flip messages with a directional spring slide, Esc to return to inbox, and a faint 'n of total' progress indicator. Make triage feel like flipping through cards in Things/Linear — effortless and fast.

Verdict-aware ambient framing: a very subtle one-time tint/glow on the reading surface keyed to the risk token (e.g. a faint top edge gradient in risk-quarantine for likely phishing, nothing for safe). Reserved strictly for real risk, it gives the page an emotional temperature without alarm-red walls — calm for safe, quietly tense for phishing.

Sender trust card on hover/expand: a monogram avatar + an expandable 'About this sender' (domain, SPF/DKIM/auth result if available, first-seen) that slides open under the header. Turns the static from-line into a confidence-building identity check — the moment a user decides whether to trust the message.

Animated verdict-change feedback after re-scan or manual review: when the user marks Safe/Phishing or a re-scan changes the bucket, the VerdictBanner morphs (color + icon cross-fade with a single spring settle) and a Sonner toast confirms, so the security state change feels deliberate and earned rather than a silent swap.

findings.area: Security verdict UI (VerdictBanner, ScanDetails, RiskBadge, ReviewActions)
findings.currentStateSummary: This surface is competent and clean but reads as a generic shadcn/ui dashboard, not a calm, authoritative security verdict. The verdict — the single most important thing the user reads — is a small 13px banner with a 16px icon and the same visual weight as everything else; it never establishes itself as the hero. Scan explainability is a stack of four undifferentiated cards (AI summary, score bars, triggered rules, optional fallback warning) with flat 24px CSS transitions and no progressive disclosure of the verdict's reasoning. Review actions are two equal outline buttons whose feedback is a literal "✓" appended to the label and a possible inline error string — no toast, no spring, no tactile press. Motion throughout is tween-based (easeOut/easeInOut, 200ms) with zero spring physics, so nothing feels physical or premium. Color discipline is mostly good (risk tokens are centralized), but ReviewActions references text-risk-phishing for the "Phishing" affordance which is the darkest #b91c1c red, slightly off the rose quarantine language used elsewhere.

findings.title: The verdict banner is not the hero — it whispers when it should speak with calm authority
findings.current: A flex row, rounded-xl, px-4 py-3, with a 16px (h-4 w-4) icon, a 14px (text-sm) label, an 11px source pill, and a 12px (text-xs) description. It enters with a 200ms easeOut fade/slide of just -4px y. It sits in EmailDetailPage.jsx:124 directly above the subject, with the exact same visual altitude as the subject block and every Card.
findings.problem: On the heart of a security product, the verdict is the answer the user came for, yet it has the same type size and chrome as a list item. There is no scale, no presence, no moment. Apple-grade hierarchy would make this the unmistakable focal point. The -4px/200ms entrance is imperceptible and generic.
findings.recommendation: Make the banner a true hero band. Use a 2-line layout: icon in a 40px tinted circle (rounded-full, bg uses tone soft + ring-1 of tone/30), label at text-lg/600 with -0.01em tracking, description at text-sm text-muted-foreground (line-height 1.5). Padding px-5 py-4, rounded-2xl. Add a 3px left accent using border-l-[3px] in the tone color for instant scannability. Replace the entrance with a spring: { type: 'spring', stiffness: 420, damping: 34, mass: 0.8 }, initial { opacity: 0, y: 8, scale: 0.985 }. Keep deference: for safe/reviewed_safe keep it visually quiet (no glow); reserve the spring 'settle' and any subtle pulse for quarantine/confirmed_phishing only.

findings.title: Strong-risk states get no visual escalation — calm is right, but quarantine/phishing must still command attention
findings.current: Every bucket renders identically: same className (tone.soft = soft bg + tone text + tone/30 border), same icon size, same padding. A 'Confirmed phishing' (#b91c1c) banner looks structurally identical to a 'Safe' (#34c77b) banner — only the hue differs.
findings.problem: The lens is explicitly 'calm authority, avoid alarm-red overload' — but the inverse failure is also present: a likely-phishing verdict carries no more weight than a clean one. Premium security UI modulates presence by stakes without shouting. Right now nothing tells the eye 'this one matters more.'
findings.recommendation: Introduce a one-line emphasis map keyed by bucket, not new colors. For quarantine/confirmed_phishing: add ring-1 ring-{tone}/25 and a subtle layered shadow (shadow-[0_8px_30px_-12px_var(--color-risk-quarantine)] at ~15% via color-mix). For safe/reviewed_safe: drop to bg-card/60 with only the left accent — recede fully. needs_review sits between. This is depth and deference doing the talking instead of saturation. No blinking, no full-bleed red fills.

findings.title: Review action buttons have weak affordance and amateur feedback (text '✓' + no toast/spring)
findings.current: Two equal flex-1 outline buttons. Icons are colorized via text-risk-safe / text-risk-phishing. Confirmed state appends a literal '✓' to the label ('Safe ✓') and swaps variant to secondary/destructive. The only feedback on success is the appended checkmark plus a full reload via onReviewed→load(); errors render as a 12px text-destructive line (ReviewActions.jsx:59-61). No Sonner toast is fired despite the stack including it — grep of the security dir and actionsApi finds zero toast calls.
findings.problem: Marking an email phishing is a consequential, satisfying action (it can move the message to Gmail Spam). It deserves tactile, confident feedback. A glyph baked into a string is not Apple-grade; it can't animate and reads as a placeholder. No press feedback, no spring, no toast confirmation, and a hard reload makes the whole panel flicker rather than the button transitioning to its confirmed state.
findings.recommendation: 1) Add a press affordance to Button (button.jsx): active:scale-[0.97] and transition timing-function cubic-bezier(0.34,1.56,0.64,1) ~150ms. 2) Replace the string '✓' with an animated lucide Check that springs in (scale 0→1, stiffness 500 damping 30) and an AnimatePresence crossfade between idle/confirmed icon. 3) Fire Sonner toasts on success: toast.success('Marked safe') and a richer toast for phishing ('Marked as phishing · Moved to Gmail Spam') so the side-effect is surfaced as a result, not buried as a hint at line 54-58. 4) Optimistically flip the button to confirmed before the network resolves instead of full load().

findings.title: No spring physics anywhere — all motion is flat tween (easeOut/easeInOut 200ms)
findings.current: Banner entrance is transition={{ duration: 0.2, ease: 'easeOut' }}. Scan-details collapse is { duration: 0.2, ease: 'easeInOut' }. A repo-wide grep for spring/stiffness/whileTap/whileHover returns nothing across the entire frontend src.
findings.problem: Linear/eased tweens feel mechanical. Apple's signature 'effortless' quality comes from spring-physics motion that has weight and settles naturally. The single most important reveal in the product (the verdict) and the explainability expand both move like a CSS demo, not a premium product.
findings.recommendation: Create a shared motion token module (e.g. src/lib/motion.js) exporting springs: SPRING_SNAPPY { type:'spring', stiffness:420, damping:34 } for the banner/badge, SPRING_SOFT { type:'spring', stiffness:260, damping:30 } for panel/height transitions. Apply SPRING_SOFT to the ScanDetails collapse in EmailDetailPage.jsx:258 (height+opacity springs read far more organically than easeInOut). Respect prefers-reduced-motion by falling back to a 120ms opacity-only tween.

findings.title: Explainability is four flat, equal-weight cards — the AI 'why' should be the centerpiece, not a peer of the score bars
findings.current: ScanDetails renders a vertical stack with space-y-4: optional amber fallback warning, AI/rule explanation Card, Risk score Card with three ScoreBars, and Triggered rules Card. Every card is the same rounded-xl border bg-card shadow-sm primitive; the only differentiation is the AI card's border-primary/25 bg-primary/5. Section icons are all 16px muted.
findings.problem: The plain-language explanation is the product's reason to exist (explainable AI for phishing) but it competes visually with raw score bars and a rule list. There's no narrative order from 'what we concluded' → 'why, in words' → 'the evidence.' It reads as a settings dump, not a confident, legible explanation.
findings.recommendation: Restructure into a clear hierarchy: (a) the AI explanation gets larger, more breathing room — summary at text-[15px] leading-7, with the Sparkles in a tinted chip, and treat it as the primary panel (not a same-size card). (b) Demote score bars + triggered rules into one secondary 'Evidence' group under a single quieter header, collapsed by default (progressive disclosure) since most users only need the sentence. (c) Stagger the children on expand with a 40ms delayChildren / staggerChildren so the evidence cascades in. This puts content first (deference) and makes the explanation feel authored.

findings.title: Score bars are thin, color-flat, and animate with a generic transition-all — they don't read as confident data
findings.current: ScoreBar is a 6px (h-1.5) track (bg-muted) with a fill colored bg-primary / bg-chart-3 / bg-chart-1, width set inline as a % with className 'transition-all'. Total score uses brand blue, Rule signals amber, AI signals blue — none mapped to the verdict's risk tone. The value sits as plain tabular-nums text above.
findings.problem: transition-all on a width is a layout-thrash smell and animates nothing meaningfully on mount. The bars are too thin to feel substantial, and coloring 'Total score' brand-blue divorces the headline number from the verdict's risk color, weakening the trust signal. There is no fill-in animation when the panel opens.
findings.recommendation: Bump track to h-2, rounded-full. Color the Total score fill with the verdict tone (verdictMeta.tone.bar) so the number and the verdict agree chromatically; keep rule/AI sub-bars in neutral chart hues. Animate the fill with framer-motion: <motion.div initial={{width:0}} animate={{width: pct%}} transition={SPRING_SOFT}> instead of transition-all. Add a faint inner highlight (after:bg-gradient-to-b from-white/10) for tactility. Right-align value at text-sm font-semibold tabular-nums to read as a metric.

findings.title: RiskBadge has no motion, no press/hover state, and inconsistent label logic across sizes
findings.current: A static span: inline-flex, rounded-full, tone.soft, two size tiers (sm: px-2 py-0.5 text-[11px]; default px-2.5 py-1 text-xs). It has a SM_LABELS override that shortens only confirmed_phishing→'Phishing' and reviewed_safe→'Reviewed' at sm size, so the label text silently changes between contexts. No transition, no entrance.
findings.problem: The badge is the most-repeated trust atom (inbox rows + header) and it's completely inert — it never animates in when a scan completes, and it has no hover identity. The size-conditional relabeling means the same email reads 'Confirmed phishing' in one place and 'Phishing' in another, eroding the calm consistency a security tool needs.
findings.recommendation: Add a subtle mount spring when the bucket resolves (scale 0.9→1, opacity, SPRING_SNAPPY) so a freshly-scanned verdict 'lands.' Add a hovered tooltip (radix) exposing the full risk description from getRiskMeta so the short label is always backed by truth. Unify labels: keep one canonical label and only truncate via CSS/width, or make SM_LABELS a deliberate, documented compact set used consistently. Add ring-1 ring-{tone}/20 for a crisper edge at small sizes on the dark bg.

findings.title: Phishing affordance uses #b91c1c (text-risk-phishing) while the rest of the danger language is rose #f43f5e — chromatic mismatch
findings.current: The 'Phishing' button icon uses text-risk-phishing (#b91c1c, the darkest confirmed-phishing red). The quarantine/likely-phishing bucket — the dominant 'danger' color a user sees in banners and badges before they act — is rose #f43f5e (risk-quarantine).
findings.problem: The mark-phishing CTA is the action that produces a confirmed_phishing state, so #b91c1c is technically defensible, but on a dark bg #b91c1c is muddy and low-contrast as an accent next to neutral text, and it visually disagrees with the brighter rose the user has been reading as 'danger.' It looks like a token slip rather than a decision.
findings.recommendation: Decide intentionally: either (a) use the rose quarantine tone for the CTA icon to match the danger language the user already associates with risk, reserving #b91c1c only for the post-confirmation state; or (b) keep #b91c1c but verify contrast (it sits ~3:1 on #0a0d14) and pair it with the destructive button fill on confirm. Document the choice in DECISIONS.md so future surfaces stay consistent. Do not leave it as an unexplained one-off.

findings.title: Ollama-fallback warning is a raw amber div using hardcoded amber-* instead of the risk-review token
findings.current: When the AI is unavailable, a div with border-amber-500/30 bg-amber-500/10 text-amber-400 and an AlertTriangle is shown, and the explanation card downgrades to text-muted-foreground. amber-500/amber-400 are Tailwind defaults, not the design system's --color-risk-review (#f0b429).
findings.problem: CLAUDE/lib conventions say never hardcode risk colors — yet this advisory uses off-palette amber that differs from the system's review/suspicious yellow, creating two competing 'caution' yellows. It also reads as a mild alarm when it's really a neutral system-status note ('explanation came from rules, not AI').
findings.recommendation: Reframe as a calm info note, not a warning: use the muted/elevated surface (bg-muted/40, border-border, text-muted-foreground) with an Info icon, or if you want a tint, use the risk-review tokens (bg-risk-review-soft, text-risk-review, border-risk-review/30) for palette consistency. Keep it to one quiet line. This is deference — system plumbing shouldn't borrow the danger register.

findings.title: Source label ('Auto scan' / 'Manual review') is an orphaned 11px gray string with no shape or meaning
findings.current: verdictSource renders as a bare 11px text-muted-foreground span inline after the label, with no separator, container, or icon.
findings.problem: Provenance — did a human or the scanner decide this? — is meaningful trust metadata in a security tool, but it's presented as throwaway gray text crammed next to the label, easy to miss and visually noisy.
findings.recommendation: Render it as a small pill: rounded-full, px-2 py-0.5, text-[11px], bg-muted/60 text-muted-foreground, with a tiny icon (ScanLine for auto, UserCheck for manual). Right-align it (ml-auto) so the label owns the left. For 'Manual review' specifically, tint it with the safe/review tone to reinforce that a person vouched for it.

findings.title: Triggered-rule rows are flat list items; points badges don't encode severity
findings.current: Each rule is a row with border-border/60 bg-background/40, the humanized rule name on the left and a muted '+N' Badge on the right. Reasons (string fallback) render as bullet '•' lines in muted text. 'Show N more' is an underlined gray text button.
findings.problem: Every rule looks equally severe; a +30 high-risk signal and a +2 nudge are indistinguishable. This is the evidence layer of an explainable-AI product and it conveys no weighting. The plain-bullet reasons fallback looks markedly cheaper than the styled rule rows, so the UI quality depends on which data path the backend took.
findings.recommendation: Map points to a subtle severity accent on each row: a 3px left bar or a colored dot whose tone steps from risk-unscanned→review→quarantine as points climb (e.g. <8 neutral, 8-19 review, 20+ quarantine). Sort rules by points desc so the strongest evidence reads first. Style the reasons fallback identically to rule rows (same chrome, no raw bullets) so quality is path-independent. Make 'Show N more' a real ghost button with a chevron and stagger the newly revealed rows in.

findings.title: Phishing side-effect (moves to Gmail Spam) is disclosed only after the fact, as a hint
findings.current: The note 'Marking as phishing also tries to move the message to Gmail Spam.' renders only once reviewedPhishing is already true (after the action ran).
findings.problem: A destructive, irreversible-feeling side effect is revealed only after the user committed to it. Premium UX sets expectations before the consequential tap, and confirms the result clearly after.
findings.recommendation: Show the consequence as quiet helper text under the buttons before action (always visible when not yet reviewed), e.g. 11px muted: 'Marking phishing moves this to Gmail Spam.' Then, on success, surface the actual outcome via the Sonner toast (see ReviewActions finding). This is the clarity principle: no surprises around consequential actions.

findings.title: Re-scan control lives outside the scan UI as a tiny ghost link, and scanning gives no progress sense
findings.current: Re-scan is a full-width ghost Button, 12px muted text, with a 14px Loader2 spinner and label swap to 'Scanning…'. It sits between the review card and the collapsible scan section.
findings.problem: Running a scan is the core action of the product, yet its trigger looks like a tertiary footer link, and the only feedback is a generic spinner with no sense of the scan actually working through the message. It under-sells the product's primary capability.
findings.recommendation: Either elevate re-scan into the ScanDetails header as a clear secondary button with a ScanLine icon, or give the in-progress state a signature: a thin indeterminate shimmer sweep across the verdict band (a 1200ms linear gradient translate) plus the spinner, so the system visibly 'thinks.' On completion, spring the new badge/banner in (ties to the RiskBadge mount finding) so a re-scan produces a satisfying, legible result.

premiumOpportunities: Signature verdict moment: when a scan completes (or re-scan resolves), play a single choreographed beat — the icon springs into a tinted ring, the risk score bars fill left-to-right with SPRING_SOFT, the badge lands with a scale pop, and (for safe only) a one-shot subtle ring 'breath.' One tasteful moment that says 'analyzed and decided,' never repeating.

Confidence meter, not a number: replace the brand-blue 'Total score' bar with a calm semicircular/linear confidence gauge colored by verdict tone, with a single plain-language anchor under it ('High confidence this is phishing'). Turns a raw 0-100 into trust.

Evidence-to-text linkage: when the AI summary references a signal ('a suspicious link to a lookalike domain'), let hovering that phrase highlight the matching triggered rule / extracted link below. Makes explainability feel intelligent and connected rather than two separate lists.

Tactile mark-phishing with undo: on confirm, animate the button to a filled confirmed state with a springy Check, fire a Sonner toast 'Moved to Gmail Spam' with an Undo action and a 5s progress ring — premium, reversible, and it surfaces the real side effect as a result.

Quiet-by-default, depth-on-demand: collapse all evidence under the AI sentence so a clean inbox is calm; expanding reveals a layered, translucent (backdrop-blur on #11151f) evidence sheet that cascades in — deference and depth working together.

Provenance timeline: a slim, elegant trail in scan details — 'Scanned 2:14pm · 7 rules · AI summary by llama3 · You marked safe 2:20pm' — giving the verdict an auditable, trustworthy paper trail without clutter.

findings.currentStateSummary: The login screen is a single centered 400px card on a dark background, with one ambient primary/10 blur glow behind it. It holds a shield-in-rounded-square brand mark, a title/subtitle, and a stacked form (email, password with show/hide eye, plus name + confirm + live password-rules checklist in register mode), a full-width submit button, a mode toggle link, and a copyright line. It is clean, conventional, and functional, but it reads as a generic shadcn/Tailwind template rather than an Apple-grade front door. The page imports framer-motion but uses NO entry motion at all — the card just appears; the only animation is the password-rules accordion using easeInOut (not spring). Field focus, button press, and brand mark are all static and flat, so the surface lacks the depth, tactility, and confident first-impression a premium security product should project.

findings.title: No entry animation despite framer-motion being imported
findings.current: The outer div and card render with zero mount animation. framer-motion's `motion`/`AnimatePresence` are imported (line 3) but only used for the password-rules list (line 214). The card and brand simply pop into existence.
findings.problem: The front door is the single most important first impression and it has no choreography. Apple sign-in screens settle in with a subtle, confident entrance. A hard pop feels cheap and template-like, and it wastes a dependency already in the bundle.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the card in `motion.div` with `initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 12, scale: 0.985 }}` `animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0, scale: 1 }}` `transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 260, damping: 26, mass: 0.9 }}`. Stagger the brand mark, title, and form with a 60-80ms `delayChildren`/`staggerChildren` via a parent variant so the card composes itself top-down rather than appearing all at once. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (framer's `useReducedMotion`) to disable transforms.

findings.title: Single flat glow reads as a stock gradient, not depth
findings.current: One `480x480` `bg-primary/10 blur-[120px]` circle pinned top-center is the entire background. The rest is flat #0a0d14.
findings.problem: Apple HIG depth comes from layered, subtly-animated atmosphere, not one static blob. A single low-opacity glow on a near-black field looks like a leftover template gradient and gives no sense of a crafted environment. For a security tool it also misses a chance to feel calm and considered.
findings.recommendation: Build a 2-3 layer ambient field: keep the cyan glow but lower it to `bg-primary/8`, add a second cooler glow bottom-right (e.g. `bg-[#1a2740]/40 blur-[140px]`), and overlay a very faint noise/grain texture (`opacity-[0.015]`) to kill banding on the near-black background. Give the primary glow a slow looping `motion` drift (e.g. translate +/-20px over 14s, `ease: 'easeInOut'`, `repeat: Infinity, repeatType: 'mirror'`) so the page breathes almost imperceptibly. Consider a faint hairline grid or radial vignette to anchor the card.

findings.title: Card backdrop-blur has nothing meaningful to blur
findings.current: Card is `bg-card/80 ... backdrop-blur shadow-2xl`. With only a single faint glow behind it, the translucency + blur are largely wasted.
findings.problem: Apple-grade translucency (materials) works because there is rich content behind the glass. Here the glass sits over near-flat black, so the effect is invisible — you pay the cost (and a slightly muddy card edge) for no perceived depth. `shadow-2xl` on a #0a0d14 background is also nearly imperceptible.
findings.recommendation: Once the multi-layer background (previous finding) exists, the blur becomes meaningful. Upgrade to `backdrop-blur-xl` and add a top inner highlight to sell the glass: e.g. a `before:` pseudo or an inset ring `shadow-[inset_0_1px_0_0_rgba(255,255,255,0.06)]` plus a real elevation shadow tuned for dark UIs `shadow-[0_24px_60px_-20px_rgba(0,0,0,0.7)]`. Consider a 1px gradient border (top lighter, bottom darker) via a wrapper instead of the flat `border-border`.

findings.title: Inputs only animate border-color on focus — no real focus presence
findings.current: Input uses `transition-colors` and on focus shows `focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:border-ring`. Height is fixed `h-10` (40px). Background `bg-background/60`.
findings.problem: `transition-colors` means the ring snaps in with no scale/glow easing, and a hard 2px cyan ring on every field feels utilitarian rather than refined. Apple fields give a soft, slightly glowing focus and a tactile feel. The 40px height is also a touch short for a hero sign-in form where fields are the main content.
findings.recommendation: On this surface, prefer a softer focus: replace the hard 2px ring with `focus-visible:ring-1 focus-visible:ring-primary/40` plus `focus-visible:shadow-[0_0_0_4px_rgba(59,158,255,0.10)]` (soft halo) and `focus-visible:border-primary/60`. Use `transition-all duration-200 ease-out` so border + halo ease together. Bump field height to `h-11` (44px, also the iOS touch target) specifically on the login form. Add `caret-primary` so the text caret matches the brand.

findings.title: Submit button has no press feedback and no width/layout stability under load
findings.current: Button is `bg-primary hover:bg-primary/90`, `h-10`, `transition-all`. On submit it prepends a spinner (`<Loader2 .../>`) before the label, so the content shifts. There is no `active:` state.
findings.problem: Premium primary buttons feel tactile: they depress on press and the loading state shouldn't jiggle the label. Here hover is only a color shift, there is no `active:scale`, and injecting the spinner before the text pushes the label right on every submit — a small but visible jank on the most important button on the screen.
findings.recommendation: Add `active:scale-[0.98]` and `transition-transform duration-150` (already has `transition-all`) to the button base, plus a brand glow on hover for the primary variant only: `hover:shadow-[0_8px_24px_-8px_rgba(59,158,255,0.5)]`. Make it `h-11` and `text-[15px]` on login. For loading, keep the label fixed and either replace it entirely (`{submitting ? 'Signing in...' : 'Sign in'}`) or absolutely-position the spinner so the label doesn't shift. Wrap in `motion.button`/whileTap for spring press if you want it consistent with the rest.

findings.title: Mode switch (Sign in <-> Create account) is a hard, jarring layout jump
findings.current: `toggleMode` flips `isRegistering`; the Name and Confirm-password fields render conditionally with no transition, the title/subtitle swap instantly, and only the password-rules list animates. The whole card height snaps.
findings.problem: Switching between sign-in and register is a core interaction on this screen and it currently feels broken — fields appear/disappear instantly and the card height jumps, drawing the eye away from the user's task. Apple transitions between such states are smooth and reassuring.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the conditional Name and Confirm fields in `AnimatePresence` with the same height+opacity pattern already used for password rules (`initial={{opacity:0,height:0}}`, spring or `duration:0.25, ease:'easeOut'`). Cross-fade the title/subtitle with `AnimatePresence mode='wait'` keyed on `isRegistering`. Animate the card height via `layout` on the `motion.div` card so the resize is a smooth spring, not a snap.

findings.title: Errors are hard-mounted and use destructive red, fighting the calm-security tone
findings.current: Error block renders with `border-destructive/30 bg-destructive/10 text-destructive` and an `X` icon, mounted/unmounted with no animation. `--color-destructive` is #ef5350 (a hard red).
findings.problem: It pops in/out abruptly, and a saturated red error on the front door reads as alarm before the user has done anything wrong. The brief says reserve strong color for real risk; an auth typo is not a security threat. There's also no `role='alert'` for screen readers.
findings.recommendation: Animate it with `AnimatePresence` (`initial={{opacity:0,y:-4,height:0}}` -> `animate`), add `role='alert' aria-live='polite'`. Soften to an amber/neutral treatment for ordinary validation (the project already has `text-risk-review` #f0b429 + `bg-risk-review-soft`), reserving destructive red only if you ever surface an actual security event. Add a subtle shake (`x:[0,-6,6,-4,4,0]`, 300ms) on a failed submit for tactile feedback.

findings.title: Typographic hierarchy is thin — only two type sizes carry the whole screen
findings.current: Title is `text-2xl font-bold tracking-tight`; subtitle and everything else is `text-sm text-muted-foreground`. Inter is loaded at weights 400/500/600/700 only.
findings.problem: Apple sign-in screens have a clear, confident scale and tend toward tighter, larger display weight for the headline. `font-bold` (700) at 24px on Inter can feel slightly heavy/generic; there's no intermediate step between the 24px title and the 14px body, so hierarchy is flat. No optical sizing or tighter tracking on the headline.
findings.recommendation: Make the headline `text-[28px] leading-tight font-semibold tracking-[-0.02em]` (semibold 600 reads more refined than bold here), and the subtitle `text-[15px] text-muted-foreground/90 leading-relaxed`. Consider Inter's `font-feature-settings: 'cv11','ss01'` or switching the display font to a tighter face for the wordmark. Add `text-balance` to the subtitle so it wraps evenly.

findings.title: Brand mark is a generic icon-in-rounded-square with no presence
findings.current: A 64px `rounded-2xl bg-primary/15 text-primary` tile containing a 32px `ShieldCheck` lucide icon. Fully static.
findings.problem: This is the visual anchor of the entire product's first impression and it looks like a placeholder — a tinted square with a stock icon, no gradient, no depth, no life. It does not establish trust or brand identity for a security product named XAI Phishing Shield.
findings.recommendation: Elevate the logo: give the tile a subtle radial/linear gradient (`bg-gradient-to-br from-primary/25 to-primary/5`), a 1px inner highlight ring (`ring-1 ring-inset ring-white/10`) and a soft outer glow (`shadow-[0_0_40px_-8px_rgba(59,158,255,0.45)]`). On mount, animate it with a spring scale-in and a one-time shimmer or a draw-on of the shield checkmark. Consider it pulsing the glow extremely slowly to imply 'active protection'. This is the #1 wow-per-effort win on this screen.

findings.title: Naming inconsistency: 'XAI Phishing Shield' here vs 'SecureInbox' as product name
findings.current: Copy and footer say 'XAI Phishing Shield'; index.html title is also 'XAI Phishing Shield', but the project/product is documented as 'SecureInbox'. The wordmark is never actually shown as text next to the logo — only in the body copy.
findings.problem: The front door should state the product name with confidence next to the mark. Right now the brand name only appears buried in a subtitle sentence and the footer, and it conflicts with the SecureInbox naming used across the codebase/docs. This undermines trust and polish.
findings.recommendation: Decide on one name and show it as a proper wordmark directly under/beside the logo (e.g. `SecureInbox` with the descriptor as the subtitle). Keep the subtitle for the value prop ('AI-powered phishing protection for Gmail'). Align index.html `` and footer to the same name.

findings.title: Password show/hide toggle button lacks focus ring and tactile feedback
findings.current: The eye toggle is a bare `<button>` with `transition-colors hover:text-foreground` and an aria-label, but no `focus-visible` style and no press state.
findings.problem: Keyboard users get no visible focus indicator on a real interactive control (accessibility gap), and it only changes icon color on hover — no scale/tap feedback. On a security form, the reveal control should feel deliberate.
findings.recommendation: Add `rounded-md focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-primary/50` and `active:scale-90 transition-transform`. Optionally cross-fade Eye/EyeOff with `AnimatePresence mode='wait'` and a 120ms fade so the icon swap isn't a hard cut. Ensure a hit area of at least 36px (`p-1 -m-1`).

findings.title: Password-rules checklist transition is generic and the satisfied state is undersold
findings.current: Rules list animates height+opacity over `duration: 0.2, ease: 'easeInOut'`. Each rule toggles between `text-muted-foreground` + X and `text-risk-safe` + Check, with no per-item transition. Lives in a flat `bg-muted/40` box.
findings.problem: easeInOut height animations on lists look mechanical; and each rule flips state with a hard color/icon swap, missing the satisfying 'tick' moment that makes password creation feel rewarding (an Apple hallmark of micro-delight). The container is a plain gray box.
findings.recommendation: Use a spring for the container reveal (`type:'spring', stiffness:300, damping:30`). Animate each rule's check with `AnimatePresence`/`motion` — a quick `scale` pop (`0.6 -> 1`, spring) and color crossfade when it turns true. Add an overall strength meter bar above the list (color ramps unscanned -> review -> safe using existing risk tokens) so progress is glanceable. Style the container as glass (`bg-white/[0.03] border border-white/5`) instead of `bg-muted/40`.

findings.title: No autofocus and no Enter-key affordance hints on the form
findings.current: Email input has `autoComplete='email'` but no `autoFocus`. The form submits on Enter (native), which is fine, but nothing guides the user's first action.
findings.problem: Apple-grade sign-in puts the cursor where the user needs it. Without autofocus, every user must click the email field first — a small friction on the most-used path.
findings.recommendation: Add `autoFocus` to the email Input (and switch focus target appropriately when toggling to register, where Name becomes first). Keep it from firing on the SSR/redirect path. Optionally add `inputMode='email'` on the email field for mobile keyboards.

findings.title: Footer copyright competes with the card and dilutes the minimal feel
findings.current: A full copyright line 'All rights reserved' sits 24px below the card in `text-xs text-muted-foreground`.
findings.problem: Apple sign-in screens are ruthlessly minimal; a legalistic 'all rights reserved' line adds visual noise and a slightly corporate-template feel to an otherwise focused screen.
findings.recommendation: Reduce to a quiet, trust-building micro-row instead of a copyright sentence: e.g. a small lock glyph + 'Encrypted - your inbox stays private' in `text-xs text-muted-foreground/70`, or links to Privacy/Terms. If a copyright is legally required, drop it to `text-[11px] text-muted-foreground/50` so it recedes.

findings.title: Loading auth state likely flashes the form before redirect
findings.current: Guard is `if (!loading && isAuthenticated) return <Navigate ... />`. While `loading` is true, the full login card renders.
findings.problem: An already-authenticated user hitting /login (or refresh) sees the entire sign-in card flash before being redirected — a jarring, un-premium flicker on the front door.
findings.recommendation: While `loading` is true, render a minimal centered brand-mark + subtle spinner (or just the logo with a breathing glow) instead of the full form, then resolve to redirect or form. This keeps the entry calm and prevents the form-flash.

premiumOpportunities: Signature 'shield activates' entrance: on mount, the logo tile springs in, the shield's checkmark draws itself (SVG path animation), and a single ring pulses outward once — establishing the 'you are now protected' feeling in under 600ms. This becomes the product's recognizable front-door moment.

Living, breathing ambient background: 2-3 ultra-slow drifting glows (cyan + cool slate) behind glass, with a faint grain overlay to kill banding. The card's backdrop-blur finally earns its keep and the screen feels alive without being busy — Apple-grade deference (content first, atmosphere recedes).

Tactile, springy mode switch: animate the card height with framer `layout`, cross-fade the headline with `AnimatePresence mode='wait'`, and stagger Name/Confirm fields in/out. The sign-in <-> register transition becomes a delightful morph instead of a layout snap.

Rewarding password creation: live strength meter bar (ramping through the existing risk tokens unscanned->review->safe) plus each requirement 'ticking' with a spring scale-pop and color crossfade. Turns a chore into a satisfying micro-interaction.

Trust-forward microcopy + glass detailing: replace the generic copyright with a quiet 'end-to-end encrypted - read-only Gmail access' reassurance, and add gradient/inner-highlight borders on the card and logo so the whole surface reads as crafted hardware-grade glass rather than a shadcn template.

Reduced-motion-aware, accessible by default: gate all spring entrances behind useReducedMotion, add role='alert' on errors, focus rings on the eye toggles, and autofocus the first field — so the premium feel never costs usability.

findings.currentStateSummary: The Reports surface is a functional but visually flat monthly summary: a right-aligned native month picker and "Email me this report" button sit above a 2-column / 3-column grid of StatCards (Synced/Scanned + 4 risk buckets), a "Top triggered rules" horizontal bar chart, and an "AI analysis" 3-up number card. The StatCards reuse the dashboard's count-up animation and are the most polished element. The chart is a barely-themed Recharts vertical bar that paints every bar the same flat blue (--color-chart-1), ignoring the rich 6-bucket risk palette, and silently discards the totalPoints metric it computes. There is no page title/header, no period context line, no last-sent feedback, and the native browser month input clashes with the otherwise carefully tokenized dark theme. Overall it reads as a "data dump" rather than an Apple-grade report you'd want to read or share.

findings.title: No page header, title, or period context — the report has no identity
findings.current: The component renders straight into a `flex ... justify-end` row containing only the month picker and send button. There is no "Reports" heading, no subtitle, and nowhere does the selected month render as a human-readable label (e.g. "June 2026"). The only month signifier is the raw `<input type="month">` value.
findings.problem: Apple-grade reporting surfaces always establish what you're looking at and for which period before showing data — clarity and hierarchy come first. Here the user lands on a wall of numbers with no title, no "Monthly security report", and no large readable month. The page also reads inconsistently with siblings; DashboardPage at least has card titles framing each block, this one opens with a bare toolbar floated to the right.
findings.recommendation: Add a real page header above the toolbar: an `h1` "Monthly report" at `text-2xl font-semibold tracking-tight`, with a secondary line showing the resolved period (`new Date(month+'-01').toLocaleDateString(undefined,{month:'long',year:'numeric'})`) at `text-sm text-muted-foreground`. Lay it out as `flex items-end justify-between` so the title sits left and the month picker + send button sit right (change the wrapper from `justify-end` to `justify-between`). Add `mb-6` / rely on AppShell's `space-y-6`.

findings.title: Chart computes totalPoints but never renders it — dead data, single-metric viz
findings.current: `data` maps each rule to `{ name, count, points }` (line 22 reads `rule.totalPoints`), but only `count` is plotted (`<Bar dataKey="count">`). `points` is computed and thrown away. The tooltip therefore only ever shows the count.
findings.problem: For a security report, 'how many times a rule fired' and 'how much risk weight it contributed' are two genuinely different stories — a rare rule worth 40 points matters more than a frequent 2-point one. The code already has the data and discards it, leaving a one-dimensional chart that under-sells the analysis. Premium data viz earns its space by saying something a number can't.
findings.recommendation: Surface points in the tooltip at minimum: pass `formatter`/`Tooltip` content showing both `count` ("times triggered") and `points` ("risk weight"). Better: add a small segmented toggle above the chart (Count | Risk weight) that swaps `dataKey` between `count` and `points`, animating the bar transition. Keep the bar `radius={[0,4,4,0]}` but ensure both metrics share the same Y-order so the toggle feels like re-weighting, not reshuffling.

findings.title: Every bar painted the same flat blue — risk palette ignored, no severity encoding
findings.current: The `Cell` loop sets `fill="var(--color-chart-1)"` (the #3b9eff brand blue) for every bar unconditionally. The project's whole identity is the 6-bucket risk palette in risk.js, yet the rules chart uses none of it.
findings.problem: A monochrome blue bar chart looks like a stock Recharts demo, not a security tool. It also wastes a free opportunity to encode meaning by color — bars could shade by the rule's average risk weight (a rule contributing 40 pts should read hotter than one contributing 2). Apple-grade charts use color intentionally; this uses it not at all.
findings.recommendation: Map fill to severity using existing tokens, not a flat color. Compute each rule's avg points-per-hit (`points/count`) and bucket it: low → `var(--color-risk-safe)` is wrong here, instead use a calm primary-to-hot ramp — e.g. <=3 `var(--color-risk-unscanned)`, <=10 `var(--color-risk-review)`, <=25 `var(--color-risk-quarantine)`, else `var(--color-risk-phishing)`. Add a subtle gradient per bar via `<linearGradient>` (e.g. base color at 0% to `color-mix(in srgb, base 70%, transparent)` at 100%) so bars have depth rather than a flat slab. Add `isAnimationActive` with `animationDuration={500}` `animationEasing="ease-out"`.

findings.title: AI analysis card colors infra failures as a security signal (amber)
findings.current: The "Failed" count renders in `text-risk-review` (amber #f0b429), the exact token used for the 'Suspicious' risk bucket. "Failed" here means "Ollama unavailable" (line 149) — an infrastructure event, not a phishing verdict.
findings.problem: This conflates two unrelated meanings of amber. A user scanning the report sees amber and reads 'risk', when it actually means 'the local AI was offline'. In a security tool, color discipline is trust — borrowing a risk color for a non-risk metric is exactly the 'drown the UI in alarm color' anti-pattern the design goal warns against.
findings.recommendation: Use a neutral/operational color for AI status. Render "Failed" in `text-muted-foreground` (like "Skipped") and instead distinguish status with a tiny dot or icon, not risk-amber. Reserve `text-risk-*` strictly for verdict counts. If you want "Failed" to draw mild attention, use `text-foreground/80` with a small `WifiOff`/`CloudOff` icon, never #f0b429.

findings.title: Native browser month input clashes with the dark theme
findings.current: Month selection uses `<Input type="month" className="h-9 w-40">`. The shadcn Input is themed for text, but `type="month"` falls back to the browser's native month picker UI (calendar popover, spinner arrows), which on most engines renders light-on-light controls and a system-blue accent that ignores --color-primary.
findings.problem: The month picker is the single most-used control on this page and it's the one element that breaks the otherwise-immaculate token discipline. The native popover looks foreign, the value formatting ("2026-06") is machine-readable not human-readable, and there's no visual hint that it's interactive beyond the border.
findings.recommendation: Replace with a custom month stepper or a shadcn Popover + month grid. Minimal-effort win: a 3-part control — `‹` prev button, a center label showing "June 2026" (`min-w-[8rem] text-center text-sm font-medium`), `›` next button — all `h-9` ghost buttons in a `border border-border rounded-md` group; disable `›` when `month === currentMonth()`. This is keyboard/click friendly, fully themed, and reads naturally. Animate the label on change with a quick `framer-motion` x-slide (12px, 180ms) in the step direction.

findings.title: Send action has no success state on the button and no last-sent context
findings.current: Clicking "Email me this report" fires `send.run`, shows a spinner in the button, then a Sonner toast on success/failure. The button label never changes, there's no checkmark confirmation, and the page never shows when/where the report was last emailed.
findings.problem: Sending a report is a deliberate, slightly anxious action (did it actually go?). A transient toast that disappears is weak confirmation for something the user can't easily re-verify (it's an email, not on-screen). Premium flows give tactile, persistent acknowledgment — the button momentarily becoming a checkmark + a quiet "Sent to you@gmail.com just now" line.
findings.recommendation: On success, transition the button to a success state for ~2s: swap icon to `Check`, label to "Sent", background to a soft `bg-risk-safe-soft text-risk-safe` (spring scale 1→1.03→1, ~300ms), then revert. Also persist a `lastSentAt`/`recipient` line under the toolbar: "Last emailed to {recipient} · {relative time}" at `text-xs text-muted-foreground`. Keep the toast but make it the secondary, not sole, confirmation.

findings.title: Double error surface: send failures show both an ErrorState block and a toast
findings.current: On send failure the catch block calls `toast.error(...)` (line 53) AND `{send.error && <ErrorState .../>}` renders a full bordered destructive panel (line 86). So a single failed send produces two simultaneous error UIs.
findings.problem: Redundant, jarring error feedback. The big destructive `ErrorState` (designed for whole-page load failures) is too heavy for a non-blocking action like 'send report', and pairing it with a toast double-counts the failure and pushes the report content down. It feels buggy, not considered.
findings.recommendation: Pick one channel. For a transient action, keep only the toast and remove the `{send.error && <ErrorState .../>}` block (line 86). If you want inline persistence, replace it with a single compact inline message next to the button (`text-xs text-destructive` with an `AlertCircle` icon) and drop the toast — don't show both.

findings.title: Chart and AI card don't animate in — entrance is inconsistent with StatCards
findings.current: StatCards have a staggered `opacity/y` entrance and count-up (StatCard.jsx:44-47). The chart and the AI analysis card just pop in with Recharts' default bar animation only; the cards themselves have no entrance, and the AI numbers don't count up like the StatCards do.
findings.problem: Within one viewport, half the elements gracefully animate in and half snap — the surface feels unfinished and the eye notices the asymmetry. Apple-grade motion is consistent and purposeful across a screen, not applied to some components and forgotten on others.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the two right-column Cards in the same `motion.div` entrance pattern as StatCard (`initial={{opacity:0,y:10}} animate={{opacity:1,y:0}}`, `duration:0.3 ease:'easeOut'`) with `delay` continuing the stagger (e.g. 0.36s, 0.42s after the 6 stat cards). Reuse the `useCountUp` hook from StatCard for the AI Evaluated/Failed/Skipped numbers so they tween like everything else. Ensure the bar chart respects `prefers-reduced-motion` by gating Recharts `isAnimationActive`.

findings.title: Chart tooltip cursor uses --color-accent and value labels are missing
findings.current: Tooltip `cursor={{ fill: 'var(--color-accent)' }}` (#1c2740) paints a full-height opaque highlight band behind the hovered bar. There are no value labels on or beside bars, so without hovering the user can't read any number.
findings.problem: The accent cursor fill is fully opaque and the same hue family as bars, so on hover it creates a muddy slab that fights the bar rather than gently indicating focus. And requiring a hover to see values fails on touch and at a glance — a report should be readable statically. Recharts default + opaque cursor = the 'default Recharts look' the brief explicitly wants avoided.
findings.recommendation: Soften the cursor to `fill: 'color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-foreground) 6%, transparent)'` so it's a faint wash, not a slab. Add static value labels via `<LabelList dataKey="count" position="right" fill="var(--color-muted-foreground)" fontSize={11} />` so every bar shows its number without hover. Round the tooltip to `borderRadius: '0.75rem'` to match card radius (`rounded-xl`) and add `boxShadow: '0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.4)'` for depth.

findings.title: Rule names truncate silently in a fixed 150px Y-axis
findings.current: `YAxis width={150}` with `fontSize: 12`. Humanized rule names (e.g. "Reply To Mismatch", "Suspicious Link Display Text") can easily exceed 150px and Recharts truncates/clips them with no tooltip on the label itself.
findings.problem: Clipped, unreadable rule labels undermine the entire point of the chart (knowing *which* rule fired). It's a clarity failure — the most information-dense axis is the one being cut off.
findings.recommendation: Either widen to `width={180}` and reduce to `fontSize: 11`, or use a custom tick renderer that wraps to two lines / adds a native `<title>` for the full name. Given names can be long, prefer a custom tick with `tspan` wrapping at ~18 chars and increase row height (`data.length * 52` instead of `* 44`) to give wrapped labels breathing room.

findings.title: Stat grid hierarchy is flat — sync metrics and risk verdicts read with equal weight
findings.current: Synced/Scanned and the 4 risk-bucket counts are all rendered as identical StatCards in two 2-col grids. The most important number in a security report (likely-phishing / confirmed) looks identical in size and weight to 'Synced'.
findings.problem: Everything-is-equal hierarchy means nothing stands out. On a security report the user's eye should be drawn first to threats found, then to volume context. Currently 'Synced 1,240' and 'Likely phishing 3' have identical visual gravity, so the scary number hides among the boring ones.
findings.recommendation: Establish a hero/secondary split. Make a single hero stat — total threats found (suspicious + likelyPhishing + markedPhishing) — at `text-4xl`, possibly spanning full width with a one-line plain-language verdict ("3 likely phishing emails caught this month"). Demote Synced/Scanned to a smaller inline 'volume' line (`text-xs text-muted-foreground`, e.g. "1,240 synced · 1,210 scanned") rather than two full cards. Keep the 4 bucket cards but tint the card border-left with the bucket color (`border-l-2 border-l-risk-*`) for instant scan-ability.

findings.title: Send button is low-affordance outline; primary action looks secondary
findings.current: "Email me this report" uses `variant="outline"` — a transparent button with just a border, same visual weight as a tertiary control.
findings.problem: The send action is the page's signature interaction (the whole 'send report' flow the brief calls out), yet it's styled as a de-emphasized outline button indistinguishable from a cancel/secondary control. Premium UIs give the primary verb on a screen clear, confident affordance.
findings.recommendation: Either promote to `variant="default"` (primary blue) so it reads as the page's main action, or keep outline but add a subtle hover lift (`hover:bg-accent` already exists) plus active press feedback (`active:scale-[0.98] transition-transform`). Tighten the label to "Email report" — "Email me this report" is wordy. Pair with the success-state animation from the earlier finding.

findings.title: Empty/zero states use raw 0s with no encouraging context
findings.current: When a month has no data, StatCards show `0` (count-up hook returns 0 immediately for zero targets, StatCard.jsx:13), the chart shows its EmptyState, and the AI card shows three zeros. There's no page-level 'nothing happened this month' framing.
findings.problem: A month full of zeros looks like an error or a broken fetch rather than the (good) news that no threats were found. The chart's EmptyState is fine, but the surrounding zero-StatCards and zero-AI-card make the page feel empty/broken rather than reassuring. Calm-confidence security UX should make 'all clear' feel like a positive result.
findings.recommendation: Detect the all-zero case (`counts.scannedEmails === 0`) and render a single reassuring panel instead of a grid of zeros: a `ShieldCheck` in `bg-risk-safe-soft text-risk-safe`, "No threats this month" / "We scanned {n} messages and everything looked safe." Reserve the full grid for months with activity. For partial-data months, keep zeros but consider rendering them in `text-muted-foreground` to de-emphasize empty buckets.

findings.title: Loading copy and skeleton mismatch — Reports uses a centered spinner, not a content-shaped skeleton
findings.current: While loading, the page shows `<LoadingState label="Building your report…" />` — a centered spinner + text (states.jsx:8-20). DashboardPage by contrast uses a `DashboardSkeleton` that mirrors its real layout (states.jsx:89-128).
findings.problem: A centered spinner causes a layout jump when content arrives and gives no sense of what's coming, whereas the dashboard's skeleton feels instant and stable. The inconsistency makes Reports feel like a lesser, older screen.
findings.recommendation: Add a `ReportsSkeleton` to states.jsx mirroring this layout: a 2-col stat grid (6 skeleton cards), a tall chart skeleton block (`h-[260px] rounded-xl`), and a 3-up AI skeleton. Swap `LoadingState` for it. This removes the layout shift and matches the dashboard's polish. Keep the nice "Building your report…" copy only if you also keep a spinner somewhere subtle.

findings.title: Card titles lack a supporting description / scale variation
findings.current: "Top triggered rules" CardTitle has no CardDescription explaining what it means; the AI card title is shrunk to `text-sm` while the rules card title is default `text-base`, so the two cards' headers don't align in scale.
findings.problem: Inconsistent title sizing between two stacked cards looks accidental, and 'Top triggered rules' is jargon a thesis examiner or new user won't parse without a one-line gloss. Clarity (Apple HIG) means labeling with a hint of meaning.
findings.recommendation: Standardize both card headers at `text-base font-semibold` and add a `CardDescription` to each: rules card → "Detection rules that fired most often this month"; AI card → "Local model (Ollama) coverage for this period". Remove the `text-sm` override on the AI title (line 135) so the two cards share a header rhythm.

findings.title: Chart container height jumps with row count and has no min/max design rhythm
findings.current: `height={Math.max(180, data.length * 44)}` — height scales linearly with number of rules (1 rule = 180px, 6 rules = 264px). The card around it has no reserved height, so the card grows/shrinks with the data.
findings.problem: Cards that resize based on data count make the page feel jittery between months and break vertical alignment with the AI card beneath. 44px/row is also tight for bars that may wrap to two-line labels.
findings.recommendation: Give the chart a stable design height — reserve a consistent card body (e.g. `min-h-[280px]`) and use 48px per row with top/bottom padding, centering the bar group vertically when fewer than 6 rules. This keeps the card height predictable month-to-month and gives bars room.

premiumOpportunities: Plain-language report headline: above the grid, render one confident sentence the user (and thesis examiner) instantly gets — e.g. "In June 2026, SecureInbox scanned 1,210 emails and caught 3 likely phishing attempts." Large `text-2xl/3xl`, with the threat count in `text-risk-quarantine`. This single line turns a dashboard into a report.

Month-over-month delta: fetch the previous month's summary and show trend chips on key stats ("Likely phishing 3 ▾ 2 vs last month") using risk-safe for improvement and risk-quarantine for worsening, with a tiny sparkline. A report's whole value is comparison over time — right now every month is shown in isolation.

Dual-metric rules chart with a Count|Risk-weight segmented toggle that springs the bars to new lengths (Framer/Recharts animated transition, ~500ms ease-out). Bars colored by severity ramp so the chart reads as a threat heatmap, not a blue list — this is the signature data-viz moment of the page.

Tactile send-report flow: button morphs Send → spinner → Check with a soft green wash and a 1.03 spring pop, then settles into a persistent "Last emailed to you@gmail.com · 2m ago" line. Optionally a one-time confetti-free 'report en route' micro-animation (a paper-plane glyph easing up-right, 400ms) for the very first send.

Shareable/exportable report: an "Export PDF" affordance next to email-send, opening a print-styled, brand-tokened layout — extremely compelling for a thesis demo ("here's the report it generates") and reinforces the 'this is a real product' feel.

Calm 'all clear' state: when a month has zero threats, replace the grid with a single serene full-width panel (large ShieldCheck in risk-safe-soft, soft radial glow, "No threats in June — you're all clear") so good news feels like a designed reward, not an empty screen.

Per-rule drill-in: clicking a bar in TopRulesChart deep-links to the inbox filtered to emails where that rule fired (the inbox already supports risk filtering), turning a static chart into a navigational, investigative surface — exactly the 'security overlay you act on' story.

findings.currentStateSummary: SettingsPage.jsx renders four shadcn Cards in a 2-column responsive grid (Profile, Gmail account, Detection & alerts, Support), each with a 16px icon + small (text-sm) title in the header. There is no page-level "Settings" title, no group-level descriptions, and the grid lets cards of very different heights sit side-by-side, producing ragged columns. The AI/alerts toggles use a small 36x20px Radix switch that animates only background-color and a 16px thumb translate via CSS transition-colors (no spring, no press feedback). The destructive "Disconnect Gmail" is a thin outline button with red text that fires the disconnect immediately on click — no confirmation, no understanding of consequences. Inputs and buttons are functional but generic; the surface reads as a developer settings panel, not an Apple-grade, grouped, deferential settings screen.

findings.title: No confirmation on destructive Gmail disconnect
findings.current: The 'Disconnect Gmail' button calls disconnect.run() directly in onClick. It is an outline button with className 'text-destructive hover:bg-destructive/10' and a Trash2 icon. One click immediately revokes the connection and reloads the account context.
findings.problem: Apple HIG treats irreversible/data-affecting actions with deliberate friction. Disconnecting Gmail wipes the only data source for the entire app (no inbox, no scans, no reports) yet it is a single, unguarded tap. There is no AlertDialog/Dialog component anywhere in src/components/ui (confirmed by listing the directory), so no confirmation primitive even exists. This is the single biggest trust failure on a security surface.
findings.recommendation: Add a shadcn AlertDialog and gate the disconnect behind it: trigger opens a dialog titled 'Disconnect Gmail?' with body 'SecureInbox will stop syncing and scanning {account.email}. Your scanned emails and reports will no longer update.' Cancel (ghost) + 'Disconnect' (variant=destructive, the SOLID red bg-destructive button, not red-text-outline). Animate the overlay backdrop-blur-sm fade 150ms and the panel scale from 0.96→1 with spring (stiffness 320, damping 30). Keep focus trapped, default focus on Cancel.

findings.title: Destructive button uses weak red-text-outline instead of a clear destructive treatment
findings.current: Disconnect uses variant='outline' with 'text-destructive hover:bg-destructive/10', so it looks identical in weight to the neutral 'Save' outline button two lines above it. The dedicated destructive variant (bg-destructive solid, button.jsx:13) is unused here.
findings.problem: On an Apple settings screen the destructive action is visually distinct and isolated (own footer row, often full-width or right-aligned, with breathing room). Here it sits flush under a Separator with the same visual weight as benign actions, so the eye doesn't register danger until read.
findings.recommendation: Inside the confirmation dialog use the solid destructive variant. On the page, present the trigger as a left-aligned ghost/link-style 'Disconnect Gmail' in text-destructive with a clear section label above it ('Danger zone' or 'Remove account'), separated by 20-24px top margin, so it is calm on the page but unambiguous when activated. Reserve the saturated #ef5350 solid fill for the confirm step only.

findings.title: No page title or descriptive header for the Settings surface
findings.current:
The component returns a fragment whose first child is the grid
. There is no

Settings

and no subtitle. AppShell.jsx provides only generic padding/centering; it injects no per-page header. Other pages (Inbox, Reports, Dashboard) also lack an h1, so the inconsistency is systemic but most jarring on Settings.
findings.problem: Apple settings screens always open with a large, confident title (Settings → grouped lists). Dropping the user straight into four cards with tiny text-sm titles gives no anchor, no hierarchy, and no sense of 'where am I'. Clarity (the first HIG principle) is missing.
findings.recommendation:
Add a page header above the grid:
with

Settings

and

Manage your account, detection, and notifications.

. Use the SF-style large-title scale: 28-30px/font-semibold/tracking-tight. Increase the grid's top spacing from the header by ~24px.

findings.title: Switch is undersized and lacks spring physics / press feedback
findings.current: Switch root is h-5 w-9 (20x36px) with a 16px thumb that translates 16px; transition is CSS 'transition-colors' on the root and 'transition-transform' on the thumb (default ~150ms ease). No scale on press, no thumb shadow change, no spring.
findings.problem: The iOS switch is the canonical tactile control: ~51x31px, a thumb that springs across and momentarily widens on press, a satisfying color sweep. This switch is small (20px tall — below the 24px comfortable hit feel), the motion is linear-feeling, and there's zero press feedback, so the AI/alerts toggles — the marquee interaction of this page — feel cheap.
findings.recommendation: Enlarge to h-7 w-[46px] (28x46px) with a 24px thumb translating 18px. Replace CSS transition with a Framer Motion thumb (animate x via spring: stiffness 500, damping 32, mass 0.8) and add active:scale-[0.97] on the root plus a slightly elongated thumb on :active (e.g. active w-[26px]). Keep data-[state=checked]:bg-primary but ease the color over 200ms. This single change disproportionately raises perceived quality.

findings.title: Group cards lack descriptions and meaningful titles read at text-sm
findings.current: Every CardHeader is 'flex-row items-center gap-2' with a 16px icon and <CardTitle className='text-sm'>. Only the disconnected Gmail state shows a CardDescription; Profile, Detection & alerts (when toggles are present), and Support headers have no description.
findings.problem: Apple groups have a clear header AND a contextual caption ('These services may use your location…'). Forcing CardTitle down to text-sm (the kit default is text-base, card.jsx:23) makes section titles the same size as body labels, flattening hierarchy. Missing group descriptions push explanatory burden onto each row.
findings.recommendation: Keep CardTitle at text-base font-semibold (drop the text-sm override) and add a one-line CardDescription under each title: Profile → 'Your display name and sign-in email.'; Detection & alerts → 'Choose how SecureInbox analyzes and warns you.'; Support → 'Reach the team directly by email.'. Set header gap to 8px, icon to a 32px rounded-md tinted chip (bg-primary/10 text-primary) for a more deliberate, iOS-grouped feel.

findings.title: 2-column grid produces ragged, mismatched-height columns
findings.current: Layout is 'grid gap-4 lg:grid-cols-2'. Profile, Gmail (tall when connected), Detection & alerts, and Support have very different heights, so on desktop the two columns are uneven and the four cards tile in source order with awkward vertical gaps.
findings.problem: Apple settings are a single, calm, scannable vertical list — not a Pinterest-style 2-col masonry that fragments related settings across columns and creates uneven whitespace. The 16px gap is also tight for premium spacing.
findings.recommendation: Switch to a single readable column with a constrained measure: 'mx-auto max-w-2xl space-y-5' (≈680px). If you keep two columns on xl, group semantically (left: Profile + Gmail; right: Detection + Support) using two flex-col stacks so heights don't fight, and bump gap to 20-24px (gap-5/gap-6). Single column is the more Apple-correct choice here.

findings.title: Toggle rows have no hover/press affordance and a cramped 12px rhythm
findings.current: SettingToggle renders 'flex items-start justify-between gap-4 py-3' inside a divide-y list. The whole row is not interactive (only the switch is), there is no hover state, and vertical padding is 12px.
findings.problem: iOS list rows feel like one tappable unit with a subtle highlight; here the label text is dead and only the tiny switch responds, hurting both feel and hit area. py-3 is tight for a 'just works' settings rhythm.
findings.recommendation: Make the row label clickable to toggle (wire onClick to onChange of the switch, or wrap in a <label>), add 'rounded-lg transition-colors hover:bg-accent/40 -mx-2 px-2' and increase to py-3.5/py-4 (14-16px). Add a faint active:bg-accent/60. Keep the divide-y but inset it so the hover highlight reads as a full row.

findings.title: Inline 'Save' buttons appear before any edit; no dirty-state or success motion
findings.current: Profile 'Save profile' is disabled until name changes (good), but the Gmail 'Save' next to maxResults is always enabled and only shows a spinner; saving surfaces a Sonner toast with no in-context confirmation. Buttons are size='sm' (h-8, text-xs) — small for a primary settings action.
findings.problem: Premium settings either auto-save (iOS) or give crisp, in-place confirmation. A persistent enabled Save with no dirty check invites no-op saves; relying solely on a corner toast for the maxResults save feels disconnected from the control that changed. text-xs buttons read as secondary chrome.
findings.recommendation: Disable the sync Save until Number(maxResults) !== account.syncMaxResults and within 1-50. On success, briefly morph the button to a check ('Saved ✓') for 1.2s before reverting, or animate a small inline check next to the field (Framer opacity+scale spring). Use size='default' (h-9/h-10, text-sm) for primary save actions so they don't read as tertiary.

findings.title: Connected-account block is utilitarian — no Gmail brand, avatar, or status pill
findings.current: Connected state shows a bordered box 'rounded-lg border border-border/60 bg-background/40 p-3' with the email in text-sm font-medium and 'Last sync: {formatDateTime}' in text-xs muted.
findings.problem: Apple's account rows show identity (avatar/initial), provider mark, and a clear connected status. Here a connected Gmail looks like a plain key/value box; there's no visual signal of a healthy, live connection, which matters for a trust-centric security app.
findings.recommendation: Render an account row: 40px rounded-full avatar (Gmail favicon or a colored initial chip), email as text-sm font-medium on line 1, and a status line with a 6px solid #34c77b dot + 'Connected · last sync {relativeTime}' in text-xs. Right-align a small risk-safe pill ('Active'). Pull the relative time ('2 min ago') for warmth, with the absolute time on hover/title.

findings.title: Support textarea is hand-rolled and visually drifts from the Input component
findings.current: The message field is a raw <textarea> with inline classes ('bg-background/60 ... focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring') instead of a Textarea UI primitive; Input.jsx uses bg-background/60 too but the focus treatment and shadow differ slightly.
findings.problem: Two near-identical-but-not-equal field styles erode the 'one coherent system' feel and create drift the moment Input changes. No Textarea component exists in the kit.
